prompts.question: Explain why an inclined plane allows a heavy object to be moved to a higher level with less force than lifting it straight up, ignoring friction.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A heavy stone must be moved up to a platform. It can be lifted straight up, or pushed up a long smooth ramp that rises to the same height.
markerNotes: The key idea is a longer distance for the same work, not less work.
Name the energy change: the gain in gravitational potential energy is the same for both methods.
State that the argument ignores friction, because on a real ramp the pushing force must also do work against friction.
commonStudentErrors: Says the ramp reduces the work done on the object, rather than the force needed.
Claims the object is lighter, or has a smaller weight, on a ramp.
Says the object gains less gravitational potential energy when it goes up the ramp.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Explains that the ramp spreads the force over a longer distance so less force is needed, and that the work done and the gain in gravitational potential energy are the same as lifting, ignoring friction
2 marks: Explains that the ramp spreads the force over a longer distance, so less force is needed
1 mark: Identifies that less force is needed on a ramp than when lifting

sampleAnswers.answer: The inclined plane spreads the lifting effort over a longer distance, so the force needed to push the heavy object up is less than its weight. Work done equals the force multiplied by the distance moved in the direction of the force, so pushing the heavy object up the plane does the same work as lifting it straight up. Both methods give the same gain in gravitational potential energy, provided friction is ignored.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Explains the longer distance and the equal work and energy gain, so it meets the top row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The ramp spreads the lifting effort over a longer distance, so less force is needed to move the heavy object up.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Explains the longer distance and less force, but does not discuss the work done.

sampleAnswers.answer: A ramp needs less force than lifting the heavy object straight up.
sampleAnswers.feedback: States the effect without any reason, which meets the bottom row.

prompts.question: Discuss why an inclined plane is an effective tool for moving heavy objects, as used by Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander Peoples, and how the angle of the plane and friction affect the force required.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A group needs to move a large, heavy stone a short distance up a gentle slope. They can use a long, gentle ramp, a shorter, steeper ramp, or a ramp with a rough surface.
keywords: Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander Peoples
markerNotes: Discuss must weigh the trade-off: a gentler angle lowers the force along the plane but increases the distance.
Treat friction as increasing the force needed, not as an unrelated complication.
Keep the link to Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander Peoples general and grounded in the physics, rather than asserting details of particular communities.
commonStudentErrors: States that a ramp reduces the work done on the object.
Says a steeper ramp always makes the object easier to move.
Gives a history of a specific community without linking it to the physics.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Discusses how the plane spreads the force over a longer distance, how the angle and friction change the force required, and makes a judgement about the most effective combination
4 marks: Discusses the effect of the angle and friction on the force required, with a clear link to moving heavy objects
3 marks: Describes how an inclined plane reduces the force needed to move a heavy object, with some reference to angle or friction
2 marks: Identifies that an inclined plane reduces the force needed to move a heavy object
1 mark: Identifies a relevant feature of an inclined plane

sampleAnswers.answer: An inclined plane is effective because it spreads the lifting effort over a longer distance, so the force needed along the plane is less than the weight of the heavy object. The angle of the plane controls this trade-off: a gentler angle needs less force, but the object must travel further. Friction acts along the surface, opposing the motion, so it increases the force required, and a smooth or well-prepared surface makes the plane more effective. The same physics explains how Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander Peoples used inclined planes to move heavy objects: an effective plane balances a gentle angle and a low-friction surface against the extra distance the object must travel.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Discusses the longer distance, the trade-off from the angle and the effect of friction, and reaches a judgement about the most effective plane, meeting the top row.

sampleAnswers.answer: An inclined plane reduces the force needed to move a heavy object, because the object moves a longer distance. Friction increases the force needed.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes the reduced force and refers to friction, but does not discuss the angle or reach a judgement.

sampleAnswers.answer: An inclined plane helps move a heavy object.

dotPoints.description: Conduct a laboratory experiment to analyse the relationship between the angle of an inclined plane and the acceleration of an object

prompts.question: Outline a laboratory method to analyse the relationship between the angle of an inclined plane and the acceleration of a trolley, identifying the independent, dependent and controlled variables.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student has a trolley, a smooth ramp with an adjustable angle, a motion sensor and a measuring tape. The student releases the trolley from rest at several ramp angles and records its motion.
markerNotes: Name the role of each variable: the independent variable is changed, the dependent variable is measured and the controlled variables are kept the same.
Repeated trials at each angle let the results be checked for consistency.
State how the acceleration is found, such as from the gradient of a speed-time graph.
commonStudentErrors: Lists the angle as a controlled variable rather than the independent variable.
Changes the mass of the trolley as well as the angle, so the effect of the angle cannot be isolated.
Gives no way of measuring the acceleration.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Outlines a method that releases the trolley from rest at several angles, measures its acceleration, and identifies the angle as the independent variable, acceleration as the dependent variable and at least two controlled variables
3 marks: Outlines a method that changes the angle and measures acceleration, and names the independent and dependent variables
2 marks: Outlines a basic method that changes the angle and measures the motion of the trolley
1 mark: Identifies the angle of the inclined plane as a variable in the investigation

sampleAnswers.answer: Set the ramp to one angle and release the trolley from rest at the same starting point, recording its motion with the motion sensor. Repeat for several angles, with several trials at each. The angle of the inclined plane is the independent variable, and the acceleration of the trolley, found from the gradient of its speed-time graph, is the dependent variable. The mass of the trolley, the length of the ramp and the surface of the ramp are controlled variables, so only the angle changes between trials.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Gives a complete method with repeated trials and names all three variables with their roles, meeting the top row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Change the angle of the inclined plane, release the trolley from rest and measure its acceleration each time.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes a method that changes the angle and measures acceleration, but names no variables.

sampleAnswers.answer: The angle of the plane is the variable being changed.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies the angle as a variable, which meets the bottom row.

prompts.question: Discuss the limitations of an experiment that measures the acceleration of a trolley on an inclined plane at several angles, including the effect of friction, and suggest how each limitation could be reduced.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A class records the acceleration of a trolley on a ramp at five angles. Their results do not show the expected pattern at the smallest angles, and the trolley is not always released from rest at the same point.
markerNotes: Each limitation needs its effect on the measured acceleration, not only its name.
A suggested improvement should match the limitation it addresses, such as a smoother ramp for friction.
Friction matters most at small angles, where the component of weight along the slope is small.
commonStudentErrors: Lists limitations without saying how they change the results.
Suggests a remedy that does not address the limitation named, such as adding mass to the trolley to reduce friction.
Says the experiment is limited because it is hard to do, without a physics reason.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Discusses two or more limitations, such as friction and inconsistent release, explaining how each affects the measured acceleration and suggesting a sound way to reduce it
4 marks: Discusses limitations with clear effects on the measured acceleration, and suggests a way to reduce at least one
3 marks: Describes two limitations of the method and their effect on the results
2 marks: Identifies a limitation of the method, such as friction
1 mark: Identifies a relevant feature of the experiment

sampleAnswers.answer: Friction between the trolley and the ramp, and within the wheels, opposes the motion, so the measured acceleration is less than the value for a frictionless inclined plane. This limitation is greatest at small angles, where the component of weight along the slope is small compared with the friction. It can be reduced by using a smoother ramp, lubricating the wheels lightly and checking that the friction is similar at each angle. A second limitation is inconsistent release: if the trolley is not started from rest at the same point, the distance covered and the timing of its motion vary, making the measured acceleration less reliable. A fixed release point or a motion sensor reduces this error, and repeating each angle several times shows whether the results are consistent.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Discusses two limitations, explains how each affects the acceleration and suggests a matching improvement for each, meeting the top row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Friction between the trolley and the ramp opposes the motion, so the measured acceleration is less than predicted. Releasing the trolley from different points also makes the results less reliable.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes two limitations and their effect on the results, but gives no way to reduce them.

sampleAnswers.answer: Friction is a limitation of the experiment.

dotPoints.description: Compare conservative forces and non-conservative forces

prompts.question: Compare conservative forces and non-conservative forces by describing how the work done by each depends on the path an object takes between two points, giving one example of each.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A box is moved from one point to another along two different paths: one straight across a level floor with friction, and one up and down a hill.
markerNotes: A comparison needs a contrast on the same point: whether the work done depends on the path taken.
Give one example of each type, and say why it belongs in its category.
Path dependence is the key idea, so 'energy is used up' is not a precise enough reason.
commonStudentErrors: Says conservative forces are the ones that conserve energy, without explaining work and path.
Says non-conservative forces destroy energy, rather than transferring it to thermal energy and sound.
Gives gravity as an example of a non-conservative force.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Compares conservative and non-conservative forces by describing how the work done depends on the path, and gives a correct example of each
3 marks: Compares the two types of force by describing the path dependence of work, without a complete example for each
2 marks: Describes conservative forces and non-conservative forces with a correct statement about path or energy
1 mark: Identifies one example of a conservative or non-conservative force

sampleAnswers.answer: Conservative forces do work that depends only on the starting and finishing positions of an object, not on the path taken, so the energy they transfer can be recovered as mechanical energy. Gravity is an example: the work done by gravity depends only on the change in height. Non-conservative forces do work that depends on the path taken, and the energy they transfer is lost to thermal energy and sound. Friction is an example, since the work done against friction increases with the distance the box travels along the path.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Compares the two forces through the path dependence of work and gives a correct example of each, meeting the top row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Conservative forces, such as gravity, do the same work whatever path is taken between two points. Non-conservative forces, such as friction, do work that depends on the path taken.

prompts.question: Analyse the energy transformations of a box sliding down a rough ramp, identifying the conservative and non-conservative forces acting on it and explaining why its mechanical energy is not conserved.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A box slides from rest at the top of a rough ramp to the bottom. The ramp is not frictionless, so the box's speed at the bottom is less than it would be on a smooth ramp of the same height.
markerNotes: Name the energy stores at the start and at the bottom, then state the transformation between them.

sampleAnswers.answer: As the box slides down, its gravitational potential energy decreases and is transformed into kinetic energy and thermal energy. The box is acted on by two forces: gravity, one of the conservative forces, and friction, one of the non-conservative forces. The work done by gravity depends only on the change in height, so gravity does not reduce the total mechanical energy of the box. Friction depends on the path travelled and does negative work on the box, transferring mechanical energy to thermal energy in the box and the ramp. Because that energy leaves the box's mechanical energy, the total mechanical energy is not conserved, and the box reaches the bottom with less kinetic energy than on a smooth ramp.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Traces the energy transformations, identifies both forces by type and explains the energy lost, meeting the top row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Total mechanical energy is not conserved for the skier. However, friction between the skis and the snow, and air resistance, are non-conservative forces. They do negative work on the skier, transferring mechanical energy to thermal energy and sound. Some of the energy is therefore lost from the total mechanical energy, so the speed at the bottom is less than it would be with no friction or air resistance. The conditions for conservation are not met, so the total mechanical energy at the bottom is less than the energy at the top.

The weight and normal force on each trolley are vertical and balanced, and with a frictionless track there is no net external horizontal force. The two trolleys therefore form an isolated system, so their total momentum is conserved during the collision, and the total momentum after the collision equals the total momentum before it. prompts.question: Describe a practical investigation, using two trolleys on a level track, that tests whether momentum is conserved in a collision. Identify the measurements needed and one source of error.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A class has two trolleys, a level track, light gates or a motion sensor, and a set of masses. The trolleys are set up to collide, and they may stick together or separate after impact.
markerNotes: Name each measurement and how it is taken: the mass of each trolley and its velocity before and after the collision.
The conclusion comes from comparing total momentum before and after, within the measurement uncertainty.

prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Describes a complete investigation with masses and velocities measured before and after the collision, a comparison of total momentum, repeated trials, and a named source of error
3 marks: Describes a method that measures velocities before and after the collision and compares total momentum, without naming a source of error

sampleAnswers.answer: Place two trolleys on a level track, with one trolley stationary. Launch the other so that it collides with the stationary one, and measure each trolley's mass and its velocity just before and after the collision using light gates or a motion sensor. Compare the total momentum before the collision with the total momentum after it for each trial, to test the conservation of momentum within the uncertainty of the measurements. Repeat the trials to check consistency. A source of error is friction on the track, which removes momentum from the trolleys, and timing error in the light gates, which affects the measured velocities.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Gives a complete method with measurements taken before and after, a comparison of total momentum, repeated trials and a named source of error, so it meets the top row.

prompts.question: Analyse possible sources of a small difference between the total momentum before and after a trolley collision, and suggest how the investigation could be improved.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student's results show that the total momentum after a collision is slightly less than the total momentum before it, across all trials. The level track is not perfectly smooth, and the trolleys are launched by hand.
markerNotes: Separate systematic errors, such as a consistent friction effect, from random errors, such as timing noise.

sampleAnswers.answer: A slightly smaller total momentum after the collision suggests an external force, most likely friction between the trolleys' wheels and the track, which removes momentum during the collision. Air resistance on the trolleys is a second, smaller external effect. Friction and air resistance reduce the momentum of the trolleys, so the total momentum after the collision looks smaller. Random timing errors in the light gates can make the result either higher or lower. To improve the investigation, the student could use a smoother track or an air track, repeat the trials and average the readings. Checking the sensor timing against a known speed would also reduce systematic error.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Analyses friction, air resistance and random error with their effects on the momentum, and links each to a suitable improvement, meeting the top row.

sampleAnswers.answer: In a transverse wave, the oscillation of particles is up and down at right angles to the direction the wave travels, so energy transfer is along the wave while the particles return to their original positions. In both waves the particles do not travel with the wave; only the energy transfer moves along the medium.

sampleAnswers.answer: The wavelength is the distance between two successive crests, or two successive troughs. The period is the time taken for one complete oscillation of a particle. prompts.question: Analyse the relationship between the frequency, period and wavelength of a transverse wave, explaining what happens to the wavelength when the frequency increases while the wave speed stays constant.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student generates a transverse wave along a rope at a steady wave speed, and then increases the rate at which the rope is shaken, so the frequency of the wave increases.

sampleAnswers.answer: Frequency and period are reciprocals: the period is the time for one oscillation, so a higher frequency means more oscillations each second and a shorter period for each oscillation. The wave speed of a transverse wave depends on the medium, not on how the wave is produced, so it stays constant when the frequency increases. Wavelength is the distance the wave travels in one period, so at constant wave speed the wavelength is inversely proportional to the frequency. As the frequency increases, the same speed fits more oscillations into each metre, and the wavelength becomes shorter. On the rope, this means the crests are closer together after the student shakes it faster, while the wave still travels along the rope at the same speed.

prompts.question: Discuss the conditions under which the wave velocity and wavelength of water waves can be used to approximate water depth, and the limitations of this approach.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A group of people use waves approaching a sandy shore to judge how deep the water is in different places. They observe the waves in deep water offshore and in shallow water near the shore.
markerNotes: Discuss needs both the condition (shallow water) and the limitations; an answer with only one side is capped.

sampleAnswers.answer: The approach works in shallow water, where the depth is small compared with the wavelength. In this case the speed of a water wave depends on the depth of the water: the shallower the water, the slower the wave. Since the period stays the same, measuring the wavelength and the period gives the wave velocity, and this velocity can be linked to the water depth. In deep water, however, the speed depends mainly on the wavelength rather than the depth, so the relationship does not apply. Limitations include the need to measure the period and wavelength accurately, the effect of tides, which change the water depth at the time of measurement, and waves that are not regular enough to give a clear wavelength. The estimate is therefore approximate, and it works best where the waves are regular and the water is shallow.
