Suggests using a thicker glass block without explaining how it improves accuracy.
Names the glass block as a source of error without a reason.

sampleAnswers.answer: The accuracy of this scientific investigation can be improved by using sharp pins set well apart, so the traced line of the ray is precise, and by drawing the normal carefully with a set square. The student should repeat trials at each incident angle and average the angle of refraction, which reduces random error. A likely source of error is parallax error, which occurs when the protractor is read from an angle rather than directly above the scale. Reading the scale with the eye directly above the mark reduces this error, so the measured angle of refraction is closer to the true value. Plotting the angles of incidence against the angles of refraction for several trials also shows whether the results are consistent.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5-mark row by discussing two improvements and identifying parallax error with a clear reason. A middle answer discusses one improvement and names a source of error without explaining it.

sampleAnswers.answer: The student could repeat trials at each angle and average the results to make the investigation more accurate.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by describing one way to improve accuracy. It does not identify a source of error or a second improvement, and adding these would lift it to the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Measuring the angles could have some errors.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by giving relevant information about the investigation. It does not name a source of error, and naming parallax error would lift it to the 2-mark row.

dotPoints.description: Relate the velocity of light to the refractive index of a medium

prompts.question: Explain how the refractive index of a transparent material is related to the speed of light in that material.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student compares the speed of light in air with its speed in a glass block.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Explains that the refractive index is the ratio of the speed of light in a vacuum to its speed in the medium, so a higher refractive index means a lower velocity of light
2 marks: Explains that light travels more slowly in a medium with a higher refractive index
1 mark: Identifies that the refractive index describes a property of a medium
markerNotes: Define the refractive index as a ratio of speeds, not as a measure of how bright the material looks.
Explain that a higher refractive index means the velocity of light is lower in that medium.
Note that the frequency of the light is not changed by the medium.
commonStudentErrors: Says a higher refractive index means light travels faster in the material.
Confuses refractive index with the colour of the material.
Defines refractive index without linking it to the speed of light.

sampleAnswers.answer: The refractive index of a medium is the ratio of the speed of light in a vacuum to the speed of light in that medium. Because this ratio is larger for a denser optical medium, the velocity of light in the medium is lower. Light therefore travels more slowly through glass than through air, while its frequency remains the same.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by defining the refractive index as a ratio of speeds and explaining that a higher index means a lower velocity. A middle answer links a higher index to slower light without the ratio.

sampleAnswers.answer: A material with a higher refractive index slows light down more than one with a lower refractive index.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by explaining that light is slower in a medium with a higher refractive index. It does not define the refractive index as a ratio with the speed in a vacuum, and that definition would lift it to the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The refractive index is a property of a medium.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by identifying that the refractive index describes a property of a medium. It does not link it to the speed of light, and explaining that light is slower in a higher-index medium would lift it to the 2-mark row.

prompts.question: Analyse why light slows down when it enters glass while its frequency stays the same, and explain what this change means for the wavelength of the light.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student shines a single-colour light from a laser into a glass block and sees the beam bend at the surface. The student wonders whether the colour of the light changes inside the glass.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Analyses the velocity change by explaining that the frequency is set by the source, so the wavelength shortens in the glass as the speed falls, and links this to a higher refractive index
4 marks: Analyses why the light slows in glass, with reference to the frequency staying the same and the wavelength changing
3 marks: Explains that the light slows in glass because the refractive index of glass is higher than that of air
2 marks: Identifies that the speed of light is lower in glass than in air
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about light in glass
markerNotes: Explain that the frequency is set by the source and does not change when the light enters another medium.
Link the lower speed to the wavelength, since the question asks what the change means for wavelength.
Connect the higher refractive index of glass to the lower velocity of light.
commonStudentErrors: Says the frequency of the light falls in the glass, which changes its colour.
Says the wavelength stays the same because the light is still the same light.
Says light slows in glass because the glass absorbs the light.

sampleAnswers.answer: The frequency of the light is set by the source and does not change when the light crosses into a different medium, so its colour stays the same. The velocity of light is lower in glass than in air because glass has a higher refractive index, meaning the speed of light is reduced more by the material. Since the frequency is unchanged and the speed falls, the wavelength of the light must also become shorter inside the glass. The change in velocity therefore links directly to the change in wavelength. This is why the beam bends at the surface and keeps its colour, even though its speed and wavelength both change.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5-mark row by explaining that frequency is fixed by the source, so the wavelength shortens as the velocity falls, and linking this to the higher refractive index. A middle answer explains the slowing and the unchanged frequency but not the wavelength.

sampleAnswers.answer: Light slows in glass because glass has a higher refractive index than air, so the speed falls while the frequency stays the same.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by explaining the slowing through the higher refractive index of glass. It does not explain why the wavelength changes, and adding that would lift it to the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Glass is a transparent material.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by giving relevant information about glass, but it does not explain the change in velocity. Stating that light is slower in glass would lift it to the 2-mark row.

dotPoints.description: Solve refractive index problems using nx = c / vx, where nx is the refractive index of the medium and vx is the speed of light in the medium
Solve problems by applying the law of refraction of light using n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂
Solve total internal reflection and critical angle problems using sin θc = n₂ / n₁
Relate the change in velocity of a light wave crossing an interface to differences between refractive indices

prompts.question: Describe how the speed of light changes as it passes from air into water, and link this change to the refractive indices of the two media.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student directs a light ray from air into a container of water, at an angle to the surface of the water.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Describes that the light slows when it passes from air into water, and links this to water having a higher refractive index than air
2 marks: Describes that the velocity of light changes at the interface between air and water
1 mark: Identifies that light changes velocity when it crosses an interface
markerNotes: Name the change as a decrease in velocity, and say which medium it happens in.
Link the change to the refractive indices of the two media, since the question asks for this link.
Refer to the interface as the boundary where the change happens.
commonStudentErrors: Says the light speeds up when it enters water.
Gives the change in speed without any reference to refractive index.
Says the refractive index of air is higher than that of water.

sampleAnswers.answer: When the light crosses the interface from air into water, its velocity decreases because water has a higher refractive index than air. Each medium has its own refractive index, so the change in velocity depends on the difference between the two refractive indices. The light travels more slowly in the water, and it bends towards the normal as it enters.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by describing the slowing at the interface and linking it to the higher refractive index of water. A middle answer describes the slowing at the interface without the refractive indices.

sampleAnswers.answer: The light slows down when it enters the water at the interface.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by describing the change in velocity at the interface. It does not link the change to the refractive indices of the two media, and that link would lift it to the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Light crosses an interface between air and water.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by identifying the interface as a boundary between two media. It does not describe a change in velocity, and stating that the light slows would lift it to the 2-mark row.

prompts.question: Analyse how the change in velocity at the interface causes the ray to bend, and predict the direction of bending if the same ray travelled from the higher-index material back into the lower-index material.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A light ray travels from a material with a low refractive index into a material with a higher refractive index. The ray meets the interface at an angle to the normal.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Analyses how the lower velocity in the higher-index material bends the ray towards the normal, and predicts that the ray bends away from the normal when it returns to the lower-index material
4 marks: Analyses how the change in velocity causes the ray to bend towards the normal on entering the higher-index material
3 marks: Explains that the ray bends towards the normal when it enters a medium with a higher refractive index
2 marks: Identifies that the velocity of the light changes at the interface
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about refraction
markerNotes: Explain the bend in terms of the change in velocity at the interface, not just the refractive index.
Predict the reverse case by reversing the change in velocity.
Use the normal as the reference line for the direction of bending.
commonStudentErrors: Says the ray bends away from the normal on entering the higher-index material.
Says the velocity increases on entering the higher-index material.
Predicts the same direction of bending on the return path, without reversing the change in velocity.

sampleAnswers.answer: At the interface, the light enters a material with a higher refractive index, so its velocity decreases while its frequency stays the same. The wavefronts slow on the side that enters first, which swings the ray towards the normal. The ray therefore bends towards the normal, and the size of the bend depends on the difference between the two refractive indices. If the same ray travelled from the higher-index material back into the lower-index material, its velocity would increase, and the ray would bend away from the normal. The change in direction is reversed, following the same relationship between velocity and refractive index. The bend would be smaller if the difference between the two refractive indices were smaller, because the change in velocity would then be smaller.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5-mark row by analysing the bend towards the normal through the lower velocity and predicting the reversed bend on the return path. A middle answer explains the bend but does not predict the return path.

sampleAnswers.answer: The ray bends towards the normal because light slows down when it enters a material with a higher refractive index.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by explaining the bend towards the normal through the higher refractive index. It does not analyse how the change in velocity causes the bend, and the prediction for the return path is missing, which would lift it to the 5-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Light bends when it crosses a boundary.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by giving relevant information about refraction. It does not say which way the ray bends or why, and identifying the change in velocity at the interface would lift it to the 2-mark row.

dotPoints.description: Construct ray diagrams to show reflection from plane mirrors and refraction at a boundary

prompts.question: Describe the features a ray diagram must show to represent reflection from a plane mirror, including the normal and the two angles.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student is preparing a labelled ray diagram of a light ray striking a plane mirror at an angle to the normal.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Describes a ray diagram with an incident ray, a normal drawn at the point of incidence, and a reflected ray at the same angle to the normal, all labelled
2 marks: Describes a ray diagram showing the incident and reflected rays, without the normal or the equal angles
1 mark: Identifies the incident ray or the normal as part of a ray diagram
markerNotes: Draw the normal at right angles to the mirror at the point of incidence, and label it.
Show the reflected ray on the same side of the mirror, at an angle equal to the angle of incidence.
Label the arrows to show the direction of travel.
commonStudentErrors: Draws the normal parallel to the mirror surface.
Draws the reflected ray at the same angle to the mirror surface, rather than to the normal.
Omits the arrows showing the direction of travel.

sampleAnswers.answer: This ray diagram shows reflection from a plane mirror: an incident ray strikes the mirror at a point, with a dashed normal drawn at right angles to the mirror through that point. The reflected ray leaves the mirror on the other side of the normal, at an angle of reflection equal to the angle of incidence. All rays and angles are labelled, and arrows show the direction of travel.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by describing the incident ray, the normal and the equal reflected angle, all labelled. A middle answer describes the two rays without the normal or the equal angles.

sampleAnswers.answer: The incident ray and the reflected ray are both drawn on the same side of the mirror, with arrows showing the direction of travel.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by describing the incident and reflected rays. It omits the normal and the equal angles, and adding them would lift it to the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: A ray diagram is a drawing of a light path.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by giving relevant information about ray diagrams. It does not describe a drawing feature, and describing the incident ray would lift it to the 2-mark row.

prompts.question: Construct written step-by-step instructions that a student would follow to draw a ray diagram showing a light ray reflected from a plane mirror and a light ray refracted at a glass boundary.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student has a protractor, a ruler, a sharp pencil and a ray box, and is drawing both diagrams on the same sheet of paper for a Year 11 assignment.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Constructs complete, ordered instructions for both diagrams, including the normal at each point, the equal angles at the mirror, and the bend towards the normal on entering the glass
4 marks: Constructs instructions for both diagrams, with the normal and one of the angle rules correctly applied
3 marks: Constructs instructions for one of the diagrams, including the normal and the correct angle
2 marks: Describes a step in drawing a ray diagram, such as drawing the incident ray
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about ray diagrams
markerNotes: Order the steps so the normal is drawn before the rays at each surface.
Give the angle rule for the mirror and the bend rule for the glass boundary.
Include the labels and the direction arrows, since they are part of a complete ray diagram.
commonStudentErrors: Gives the steps for the mirror but omits the glass boundary.
Draws the refracted ray bending away from the normal on entering the glass.
Gives instructions without a normal, so the angles cannot be measured.

sampleAnswers.answer: Step 1: For this ray diagram, draw the plane mirror as a straight line and the glass boundary as a second straight line on the same sheet, leaving space between them. Step 2: At the mirror, draw a dashed normal at right angles to the surface, then draw the incident ray at the chosen angle of incidence measured with the protractor. Step 3: Draw the reflected ray on the same side of the mirror, on the other side of the normal, at an angle equal to the angle of incidence. Step 4: At the glass boundary, draw a normal, then draw the incident ray in air at the chosen angle, and draw the refraction ray bending towards the normal as it enters the glass. Step 5: Label each angle and normal, and add arrows showing the direction of travel for every ray.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5-mark row by giving ordered steps for both diagrams, including the normal at each point, the equal reflected angle and the bend towards the normal. A middle answer gives complete steps for the mirror only.

sampleAnswers.answer: Draw a dashed normal at the mirror, draw the incident ray at the chosen angle, and draw the reflected ray at the same angle on the other side of the normal.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by constructing instructions for the mirror diagram, with the normal and the equal angle. It does not cover the glass boundary, and adding the refraction step would lift it to the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: A ray diagram is a drawing of light paths.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by giving relevant information about ray diagrams. It does not describe a drawing step, and describing a step such as drawing the incident ray would lift it to the 2-mark row.

dotPoints.description: Conduct a laboratory experiment to determine the refractive index of a material and assess the accuracy of the measurement

prompts.question: Describe the method a student would use in a laboratory experiment to determine the refractive index of a glass block, including the measurements taken and the equipment used.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student has a rectangular glass block, a ray box, paper, pins, a protractor and a ruler, and must investigate the refractive index of the glass using the angles of the rays.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Describes a laboratory experiment that measures the angles of incidence and refraction from the normal for several rays, with the equipment, and explains how the refractive index is found from these angles
2 marks: Describes a laboratory experiment that measures the angles of incidence and refraction, without explaining how the refractive index is found
1 mark: Identifies some relevant equipment or a relevant measurement
markerNotes: Name both angles and say they are measured from the normal, not from the surface.
Explain that the refractive index is found from the ratio of the sines of the two angles, which is a constant for the glass.
Name the equipment used to trace the rays, such as the ray box, pins and paper.
commonStudentErrors: Measures the angles from the surface of the glass block instead of the normal.
Lists the equipment without saying what is measured or how it is used.
Says the refractive index is read directly from the glass block.

sampleAnswers.answer: In this laboratory experiment, the student traces a ray from the ray box through the glass block onto paper, with the normal drawn at the surface. The student measures the angles of incidence and refraction from the normal with a protractor, for several rays. The refractive index is the ratio of the sines of these angles, which is constant for the glass.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by describing the trace, the angles measured from the normal and how the refractive index is found. A middle answer describes the angles but not how the refractive index is found.

sampleAnswers.answer: The student shines a ray through a glass block and measures the angles of the incident and refracted rays with a protractor.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by describing a laboratory experiment that measures both angles. It does not explain how the refractive index is found from them, and that link would lift it to the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The student uses a glass block and a protractor.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by identifying relevant equipment. It describes no measurement, and describing the angles measured would lift it to the 2-mark row.

prompts.question: Assess the accuracy of the student's measurement of the refractive index, referring to at least two sources of uncertainty and how each could be reduced.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student's refractive index result for a glass block is close to the expected value, but the student measured each angle once, by eye, from a ray traced on paper with thick pins.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Assesses the accuracy of the measurement by explaining two sources of uncertainty, such as parallax error and imprecise tracing, and judging the effect of each on the refractive index
5 marks: Assesses the accuracy of the measurement by identifying two sources of uncertainty and explaining how they affect the result
4 marks: Discusses one source of uncertainty in the measurement, and how it affects the refractive index
3 marks: Explains how one source of error could change the angles measured
2 marks: Identifies a source of uncertainty in measuring the angles
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about the refractive index
markerNotes: Judge the accuracy directly, since the question asks you to assess it, and do not only list errors.
Explain how each source changes the angle of refraction and so the refractive index.
Give a reduction for each source, such as sharper pins or repeat trials, so the answer is complete.
commonStudentErrors: Lists errors without saying how they change the refractive index.
Says the result is accurate because it is close to the expected value.
Names a random error and gives no way to reduce it.

sampleAnswers.answer: The accuracy of this measurement is limited mainly by two sources of uncertainty. First, the angles were read by eye from a traced ray, so parallax error can make the protractor reading slightly wrong, which shifts the angle of refraction and so changes the refractive index. Second, thick pins make the traced ray imprecise, so the position of the emerging ray is uncertain. Because the refractive index depends on the ratio of sines of the angles, a small error in the angle of refraction has a significant effect on the result. The accuracy can be improved by using sharp pins and by making repeat trials at each angle, then averaging the results and reporting their spread as the uncertainty. A student who understands these limits reports the refractive index as a range rather than as a single exact value, which is the most accurate way to present the measurement.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row by assessing the accuracy through two sources of uncertainty, explaining the effect of each on the refractive index and suggesting reductions. A middle answer identifies one source of error and its effect on the angle.

sampleAnswers.answer: Parallax error could make the protractor reading slightly wrong, which would change the angle of refraction measured.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by explaining how one source of error changes the angle measured. It does not assess a second source or judge the effect on the refractive index, and adding these would lift it to the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The measurement could have errors.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by giving relevant information about the measurement. It does not name a source of uncertainty, and identifying one such as parallax error would lift it to the 2-mark row.

dotPoints.description: Conduct a scientific investigation to discuss how spectacles assist people with vision impairment

prompts.question: Explain how a diverging lens in spectacles helps a person with short-sightedness to see distant objects clearly.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A Year 11 student has difficulty reading the board at the front of the classroom, and an optometrist explains the vision problem as the eye focusing light in front of the retina.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Explains that a diverging lens spreads the incoming light so that the image of a distant object forms on the retina, correcting the focus in front of the retina
2 marks: Explains that a diverging lens corrects short-sightedness, without the link to where the image forms
1 mark: Identifies a diverging lens as a type of lens used in spectacles
markerNotes: Name the problem as the image forming in front of the retina, so the lens must move the focus back.
Explain that the diverging lens spreads the light before it enters the eye.
Link the correction to the retina, since the question asks how distant objects become clear.
commonStudentErrors: Says the diverging lens makes the image bigger on the retina.
Says short-sightedness is corrected by a converging lens, which is the wrong lens.
Says the lens focuses the light behind the retina.

sampleAnswers.answer: In short-sightedness, the eye's lens focuses the image of a distant object in front of the retina. A diverging lens in the spectacles spreads the incoming light rays slightly before they enter the eye, so the eye focuses the image further back, on the retina. This refraction corrects the blurred view of distant objects.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by explaining that the diverging lens moves the focus back onto the retina. A middle answer explains the correction without saying where the image forms.

sampleAnswers.answer: A diverging lens in spectacles corrects short-sightedness by spreading the light before it reaches the eye.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by explaining that the diverging lens corrects short-sightedness. It does not say where the image forms, and explaining that it lands on the retina would lift it to the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Spectacles can use a diverging lens.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by identifying a diverging lens in spectacles. It does not explain the correction, and linking the lens to short-sightedness would lift it to the 2-mark row.

prompts.question: Discuss how a scientific investigation using a converging lens, a ray box and a screen could model the way spectacles correct long-sightedness, and identify one limitation of the model.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student uses a ray box to send parallel rays through a converging lens and onto a screen, and moves the screen until the image is sharpest.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Discusses how the converging lens brings parallel rays to a focus earlier than the eye would, so the image forms on the retina, and identifies a limitation of the model such as the single lens or the flat screen
4 marks: Discusses how a converging lens brings parallel rays to a focus, linking this to long-sightedness, with some reference to the model
3 marks: Explains that a converging lens focuses parallel rays to a point, which corrects long-sightedness
2 marks: Identifies that a converging lens is used to correct long-sightedness
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about lenses
markerNotes: Compare the model with the eye, rather than only describing the lens.
Explain the correction in terms of where the focus falls relative to the retina.
Name one limitation of the model, such as a single lens or a flat screen, with a reason.
commonStudentErrors: Says the converging lens spreads the light so the image forms behind the retina.
Describes the investigation without linking it to long-sightedness.
Says the model is perfect because it works in the same way as the eye.

sampleAnswers.answer: The scientific investigation shows that a converging lens brings parallel rays from a distant object to a focal point, which is the basis for correcting long-sightedness. In a long-sighted eye, the image of a near object focuses behind the retina because the eye is too short or its lens is too weak. A converging lens in spectacles bends the incoming rays inwards before they reach the eye, so they reach a focus earlier and the image forms on the retina. The model, with a ray box, a single lens and a flat screen, has a limitation: the eye's lens changes shape and the retina is curved, so the model cannot show how the eye adjusts for different distances.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5-mark row by discussing how the converging lens brings parallel rays to a focus on the retina, and identifying a limitation of the model. A middle answer links the lens to long-sightedness without discussing the model.

sampleAnswers.answer: A converging lens focuses parallel rays to a point, so an image can be brought onto the retina for a long-sighted person.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by explaining that a converging lens focuses parallel rays to correct long-sightedness. It does not discuss the model or a limitation, and adding a limitation would lift it to the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Spectacles are lenses in a frame.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by giving relevant information about spectacles. It does not describe a lens correcting vision, and explaining how a converging lens focuses light would lift it to the 2-mark row.

dotPoints.description: Conduct a practical investigation to model how waves diffract through openings and around obstacles of different sizes

prompts.question: Describe a practical investigation a student could conduct to model how water waves diffract through openings and around obstacles, including the equipment used.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student has a ripple tank with a plane wave generator, a set of barriers with gaps of different widths, and a small obstacle that can be placed in the path of the waves.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Describes a practical investigation with a ripple tank that varies the width of openings and the size of obstacles, observes the spreading of the waves, and names the equipment
2 marks: Describes a practical investigation that varies the width of an opening or the size of an obstacle, without the equipment or the observations
1 mark: Identifies some relevant equipment or a relevant variable
markerNotes: Name the independent variable, the width of the opening or the size of the obstacle.
Describe what is observed, which is how far the waves spread past each opening or obstacle.
Name a controlled variable, such as the wavelength of the waves, so only the opening changes.
commonStudentErrors: Lists the equipment without a variable to change.
Describes a ripple tank without saying what is observed.
Says the waves bounce off the barrier, which describes reflection rather than diffraction.

sampleAnswers.answer: In this practical investigation, the student uses a ripple tank with a plane wave generator and sets barriers with openings of different widths in the wave path. The student observes how much the waves diffract through each opening, and places an obstacle in the wave path, changing its size to see how the waves bend around it. The wavelength of the waves is kept constant as the controlled variable.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by describing a ripple tank investigation that varies the openings and obstacles, observes the diffraction and names a controlled variable. A middle answer varies the opening without naming the controlled variable.

sampleAnswers.answer: The student changes the width of a gap in a barrier in a ripple tank and watches how the waves spread through it.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by describing an investigation that varies the width of an opening. It does not name the equipment or record the observations, and adding these would lift it to the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The student uses a ripple tank.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by identifying relevant equipment. It describes no variable or observation, and changing the gap width would lift it to the 2-mark row.

prompts.question: Analyse the student's observations to explain how the width of an opening, compared with the wavelength, affects how much the waves diffract.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: The student's ripple tank shows that waves with the same wavelength spread out widely after passing through a narrow gap, but pass through a wide gap with little spreading.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Analyses the observations to show that diffraction is greatest when the opening is about the wavelength or smaller, and explains that the spreading depends on the ratio of the opening to the wavelength
4 marks: Analyses the observations to show that narrower openings cause more diffraction, with reference to the wavelength
3 marks: Explains that waves diffract more through a narrow opening than through a wide opening
2 marks: Identifies that the width of the opening affects the diffraction of waves
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about waves in the ripple tank
markerNotes: Compare the width of the opening with the wavelength, since the question asks for this comparison.
Describe the wave after the narrow gap as spreading out, like a new source of waves at the gap.
Refer to obstacles as well as openings, since diffraction also occurs around them.
commonStudentErrors: Says the waves diffract more through a wide gap because more wave passes through.
Says diffraction depends on the speed of the waves, not the wavelength.
Describes the observations without explaining why the spreading happens.

sampleAnswers.answer: The observations show that the amount of diffraction depends on the width of the opening compared with the wavelength of the wave. Through the narrow gap, the wave spreads out widely, almost as if the gap were a new source of circular waves. Through the wide gap, the wave passes straight through with little spreading, because the gap is much larger than the wavelength. Diffraction is greatest when the opening is about the same size as the wavelength or smaller, and it decreases as the opening becomes much wider than the wavelength. The same principle applies around obstacles, so the waves diffract more around small obstacles, and this is why the spreading depends on the ratio of the opening to the wavelength.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5-mark row by analysing the observations through the ratio of the opening to the wavelength and extending the idea to obstacles. A middle answer explains that narrow gaps cause more spreading without the wavelength comparison.

sampleAnswers.answer: Waves diffract more through a narrow opening than through a wide opening, so the waves spread out more after the narrow gap.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by explaining the greater diffraction through a narrow opening. It does not link the spreading to the wavelength, and adding that link would lift it to the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The waves spread out after the gap.

prompts.question: Describe the principle of superposition, and how a student could model it with two pulses travelling along a rope.

sampleAnswers.answer: The principle of superposition states that when two waves overlap, the resultant displacement at each point is the sum of the individual displacements. To model this, the student sends two pulses towards each other along the rope, and at the point where they overlap the rope shows the combined displacement. After the pulses pass through each other, each continues unchanged, so the overlap is only temporary.

prompts.question: Analyse a student's model in which an upward pulse and a downward pulse of equal size travel towards each other along a rope, and explain the displacement of the rope when the pulses overlap.

markerNotes: Explain the flat shape by adding the upward and downward displacements at each point.

sampleAnswers.answer: The student's model shows the principle of superposition at work. Each pulse produces its own displacement at every point along the rope, and at the moment the pulses meet, the upward and downward displacements are equal in size and opposite in direction. Their displacements add together at each point, so the rope is flat at the instant of overlap, which is an example of destructive interference. This flat shape is only temporary. After the pulses pass through each other, each continues with its original shape and size, because the displacements combine only at the point where they overlap. This is the principle of superposition at work: the rope's displacement is the sum at each instant, and the pulses carry on with no lasting change.

dotPoints.description: Use the principle of superposition to explain the constructive interference and destructive interference of waves

prompts.question: Explain why two waves that are in phase produce constructive interference, while two waves that are half a cycle out of phase produce destructive interference.

prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Explains that in-phase waves add their displacements to give a larger amplitude, and that waves half a cycle out of phase cancel where a crest meets a trough, using the principle of superposition
2 marks: Explains that in-phase waves reinforce each other, and out-of-phase waves cancel each other
1 mark: Identifies that waves can reinforce or cancel each other
markerNotes: Explain that in-phase crests and troughs coincide, so the displacements add.
Explain that a crest meeting a trough gives destructive interference, with the displacements cancelling.

commonStudentErrors: Says constructive interference happens when waves are half a cycle out of phase.
Says destructive interference makes the waves louder.

sampleAnswers.answer: Using the principle of superposition, when two waves are in phase their crests and troughs coincide, so their displacements add and give constructive interference with a larger amplitude. When the waves are half a cycle out of phase, a crest meets a trough, so the displacements subtract and the waves cancel, which is destructive interference.

sampleAnswers.answer: In-phase waves reinforce each other, and waves that are out of phase cancel each other.

sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by identifying that waves can reinforce or cancel. It does not say when this happens, and naming in-phase and out-of-phase waves would lift it to the 2-mark row.

prompts.question: Analyse why a listener standing near two identical speakers hears alternating loud spots and quiet spots as they walk along a line, using the ideas of constructive and destructive interference.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: Two identical speakers play the same tone in phase. A listener walks slowly along a line parallel to the speakers and notices that the sound becomes louder and quieter at regular spots.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Analyses the path of the waves from each speaker, showing that the listener hears constructive interference where the waves arrive in phase and destructive interference where they arrive out of phase, so loud and quiet spots alternate
4 marks: Analyses the listener's position relative to the two speakers, linking loud spots to constructive interference and quiet spots to destructive interference
3 marks: Explains that constructive interference produces loud spots and destructive interference produces quiet spots
2 marks: Identifies that the sound is louder at some points and quieter at others
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about interference
markerNotes: Explain that the path difference to the listener changes as the listener walks, so the phase relationship changes too.
Link each loud spot to in-phase arrival and each quiet spot to out-of-phase arrival.
Mention that the pattern repeats along the line, since the spots alternate.
commonStudentErrors: Says the loud spots occur because the speakers are closer to the listener.
Says the quiet spots are caused by the sound being absorbed by the air.
Describes the loud and quiet spots without any reference to the waves arriving in phase.

sampleAnswers.answer: The waves from the two identical speakers are in phase at the speakers, and the principle of superposition applies at every point the listener can reach. At a loud spot, the waves from each speaker arrive in phase because the difference in distance from the two speakers is a whole number of wavelengths, so there is constructive interference and the displacements add. As the listener walks, the difference in distance changes, and at a quiet spot the waves arrive out of phase, half a cycle apart, so there is destructive interference and the waves cancel. Moving along the line therefore produces alternating loud spots and quiet spots, which repeat as the difference in distance changes by one wavelength.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5-mark row by analysing the in-phase and out-of-phase arrivals and the alternating pattern along the line. A middle answer explains the loud and quiet spots through interference without the path difference.

sampleAnswers.answer: A loud spot is where the waves arrive in phase and interfere constructively, and a quiet spot is where they interfere destructively.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by explaining the loud and quiet spots through constructive and destructive interference. It does not explain the change in distance or why the spots alternate, and adding these would lift it to the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Interference is a property of waves.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by giving relevant information about interference. It does not say where the sound is louder or quieter, and identifying loud and quiet spots would lift it to the 2-mark row.

dotPoints.description: Explain how the superposition of waves produces interference patterns with observable maxima and minima

prompts.question: Explain how two coherent sources of waves produce an interference pattern with observable maxima and minima.

prompts.markingCriteria:

sampleAnswers.answer: Waves from two coherent sources, which have the same frequency and a constant phase difference, overlap and combine by superposition. At points where the waves arrive in phase, the displacements add to give maxima, while at points where they arrive out of phase they cancel to give minima. The alternating maxima and minima form the observable interference pattern.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by explaining coherent sources, superposition, and the maxima and minima of the interference pattern. A middle answer describes overlapping waves reinforcing and cancelling without coherent sources.

sampleAnswers.answer: Two sources of waves overlap, and at some points the waves reinforce while at others they cancel.

prompts.question: Discuss why the interference pattern would become unstable if the two dippers were driven at different frequencies, and why the sources must be coherent for a stable pattern.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student sets up two dippers in a ripple tank, but one dipper is accidentally driven at a slightly different frequency from the other. The student observes the pattern on the water surface.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Discusses that a stable pattern needs coherent sources with a constant phase difference, and explains that different frequencies make the phase difference change, so the maxima and minima move and the pattern is unstable
4 marks: Discusses the effect of different frequencies on the phase difference and the pattern, with reference to coherent sources
3 marks: Explains that the two sources must have the same frequency to produce a stable interference pattern
2 marks: Identifies that coherent sources are needed for an interference pattern
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about the ripple tank
markerNotes: Explain that the phase difference changes continually when the frequencies differ.
Describe the maxima and minima as moving across the surface, rather than stopping.
Give the reason coherence matters: a constant phase difference fixes the positions of maxima and minima.
commonStudentErrors: Says the pattern disappears entirely because the waves no longer superpose.
Says the sources must be at different frequencies to produce a pattern.
States that coherence only affects the brightness of the pattern.

sampleAnswers.answer: A stable interference pattern needs coherent sources, which have the same frequency and a constant phase difference between them. If the dippers are driven at different frequencies, the phase difference between the two waves continually changes, so a point that was a maximum soon becomes a minimum. The maxima and minima therefore move across the water surface, and the interference pattern is unstable. Superposition still occurs at every point, but the pattern changes too quickly to observe as a steady set of maxima and minima. A constant phase difference keeps the positions of the maxima and minima fixed, so coherence is needed for the pattern to be observed and measured.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5-mark row by discussing the changing phase difference, the moving maxima and minima, and the role of coherent sources. A middle answer explains the need for the same frequency without the changing phase difference.

sampleAnswers.answer: The two sources must have the same frequency, or the pattern will not stay in one place.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by explaining that the sources must share a frequency for a stable pattern. It does not explain the changing phase difference or the movement of the maxima and minima, and adding these would lift it to the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Ripple tanks are used to show waves.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by giving relevant information about the ripple tank. It does not address frequency or coherence, and identifying the need for coherent sources would lift it to the 2-mark row.

dotPoints.description: Demonstrate the formation of a standing wave

prompts.question: Demonstrate how a standing wave forms on a string fixed at both ends, by describing the incident wave, the reflected wave and how they superpose.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student attaches a string between two fixed supports and drives one point on the string with an oscillator at a steady frequency.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Demonstrates the formation of a standing wave by describing the incident and reflected waves meeting on the string, and their superposition producing a fixed pattern of displacement
2 marks: Describes an incident wave and a reflected wave on a string, without the superposition that forms the standing wave

Describes the reflected wave as unchanged from the incident wave in every case.

sampleAnswers.answer: A standing wave forms on a string fixed at both ends because the incident wave travelling from the oscillator is reflected at each fixed end, so a reflected wave travels back along the string. The incident wave and the reflected wave undergo superposition, and at particular points they reinforce while at others they cancel. The resulting pattern stays in fixed positions along the string, which is the standing wave.

prompts.question: Analyse why a standing wave forms on a string fixed at both ends only at particular frequencies, and what the student would observe if the driving frequency were changed slightly.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student adjusts the oscillator on a string fixed at both ends, and finds that the string shows a clear standing wave pattern at some settings but not at others.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Analyses why standing waves form only when the string length fits a whole number of half wavelengths between the fixed ends, and explains that a slightly different frequency gives a poorly defined pattern because the reflected wave no longer fits
4 marks: Analyses why standing waves form only at particular frequencies, with reference to the reflected wave and the fixed ends

sampleAnswers.answer: A standing wave forms only at particular frequencies because the reflected wave must return in step with the incident wave. Each fixed end is a point of zero displacement, so the string length must fit a whole number of half wavelengths between the two ends. Only then do the incident and reflected waves superpose to give a stable pattern of nodes and antinodes. At other frequencies, the reflected wave is out of step with the incident wave when they meet, so the waves do not settle into a stable pattern. If the driving frequency were changed slightly, the standing wave would weaken and the string would show a poorly defined pattern, because the reflected wave no longer fits the string length. This is the condition of resonance.

prompts.question: Explain how nodes and antinodes are produced in a standing wave on a string fixed at both ends.

sampleAnswers.answer: A node is produced where the incident and reflected waves meet with opposite displacements, so they cancel by destructive interference and the point has zero displacement. An antinode is produced where the two waves meet in phase, so they reinforce by constructive interference and the point has maximum displacement. The production of nodes and antinodes therefore follows from the superposition of the waves in the standing wave.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by explaining both features through destructive and constructive interference with the displacement at each. A middle answer describes the motion of nodes and antinodes without how they are produced.

The nodes and antinodes become more closely spaced, because each loop is shorter, while the standing wave is still fixed at the same two ends. The positions of the nodes shift along the string as the harmonic changes. The ends of a string fixed at both ends must always be nodes, because the attachment points cannot move, so the displacement there is zero. Each higher harmonic therefore still has a node at each fixed end, with the nodes and antinodes arranged between them. These positions follow directly from the superposition of the incident and reflected waves at each point along the string.

prompts.question: Explain why the pitch of a siren on a passing emergency vehicle appears to change as the vehicle moves towards and then away from an observer.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A stationary observer stands beside a road as an emergency vehicle with a siren approaches, passes and drives away.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Explains that the source moving towards the observer compresses the sound waves, raising the frequency and pitch, and that moving away stretches the waves, lowering the frequency and pitch
2 marks: Explains that the pitch changes because the sound waves are compressed or stretched by the moving source

markerNotes: Name the frequency shift as the change in the frequency heard by the observer.
Explain that the approaching source compresses the waves and the receding source stretches them.

sampleAnswers.answer: As the vehicle approaches, its motion compresses the sound waves ahead of it, so the wavelength reaching the observer is shorter and the frequency heard is higher, giving a higher pitch. As the vehicle moves away, the sound waves are stretched, so the wavelength is longer and the frequency heard is lower. This frequency shift occurs because the source moves relative to the observer, and it is called the Doppler effect.

prompts.question: Analyse how the light from a star moving away from Earth shows a redshift, and how a star moving towards Earth shows a blueshift, in terms of the wavelength of the light observed.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: An astronomer compares the light from two stars, one moving towards Earth and one moving away from Earth, against the light from a stationary source in the laboratory.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Analyses how the motion of each source changes the observed wavelength of its light, with a receding source showing a longer wavelength and redshift, and an approaching source showing a shorter wavelength and blueshift, linked to the frequency shift
4 marks: Analyses the redshift and blueshift for both sources, with reference to the change in wavelength
3 marks: Explains that a source moving away from the observer shows a redshift, and one moving towards shows a blueshift
2 marks: Identifies redshift or blueshift as shifts in the light observed from moving sources
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about light from stars
markerNotes: Explain the shift as the motion of the source changing the wavelength received by the observer.
Name the redshift as the longer wavelength for a receding source, and the blueshift as the shorter wavelength for an approaching one.
Note that the source's own light is unchanged; only the observed wavelength changes.
commonStudentErrors: Says a star moving away from Earth shows a blueshift.
Says the wavelength of the light changes because the star becomes hotter.
Says the frequency shift applies to sound waves only.

sampleAnswers.answer: The frequency shift occurs because the motion of the source relative to the observer changes the wavelength of the light that is received. For the star moving away from Earth, the light waves are stretched, so the observed wavelength is longer and shifts towards the red end of the spectrum. This is a redshift. For the star moving towards Earth, the light waves are compressed, so the observed wavelength is shorter and shifts towards the blue end, which is a blueshift. In both cases the source's own light is unchanged. Only the wavelength received by the observer is altered by the motion of the source, and astronomers use these shifts to infer how the source is moving.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5-mark row by analysing the stretched and compressed light waves for each source and linking them to the frequency shift. A middle answer identifies both shifts without analysing the wavelength change.

sampleAnswers.answer: A star moving away from Earth shows a redshift, because its light waves are stretched and their wavelength is longer.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by explaining the redshift for a receding source. It does not describe the blueshift for an approaching source, and adding that would lift it to the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Stars give off light that can be measured.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by giving relevant information about light from stars. It does not describe a shift, and identifying redshift or blueshift would lift it to the 2-mark row.

Explain the role of the movement of electrons in charging particles and objects

prompts.question: Describe the movement of electrons that causes a plastic rod to become negatively charged when it is rubbed with a woollen cloth.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student rubs a plastic rod with a woollen cloth, and the rod then attracts small pieces of paper. Both the rod and the cloth were neutral before they were rubbed together.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Describes the movement of electrons from the cloth to the rod, with the resulting negative and positive charges on each object stated accurately
2 marks: Describes the movement of electrons, with one of the resulting charges correctly stated
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about charging by rubbing
markerNotes: Name the particle that moves: electrons move during friction charging, while protons stay fixed in the nucleus.
State the sign of charge on both objects, since the question asks for the charge on the rod.
A strong answer links the gain of electrons to a negative charge and the loss of electrons to a positive charge.
commonStudentErrors: Says protons move from the cloth to the rod, which is incorrect because protons are held in the nucleus.
Describes the rod as positive because it gained electrons, which reverses the sign of the charge.
States that the objects become charged by creating new charge, with no transfer of electrons.

sampleAnswers.answer: Both the rod and the cloth start neutral. During charging by rubbing, electrons move from the cloth onto the rod. The rod gains extra electrons and has a net negative charge. The cloth loses electrons and has a net positive charge. Protons stay fixed in the nuclei, so only the movement of electrons causes the charging.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row: the movement of electrons is described, both charges have the correct sign, and protons are correctly excluded.

sampleAnswers.answer: Electrons move from the cloth onto the rod. The rod therefore gains electrons and becomes negatively charged.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by describing the electron movement and the negative charge on the rod, but the positive charge on the cloth is not stated. Adding that charge would lift it to the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The rod and the cloth become charged when they are rubbed together.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by giving relevant information about charging, but it names no particles and gives no sign of charge. Describing which particles move would lift it to the 2-mark row.

prompts.question: Analyse the student's claim, using the movement of electrons and protons to explain whether the glass becomes positive for this reason.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student's lab report states that rubbing a glass rod with a silk cloth makes the glass positive, because protons are rubbed off the glass and onto the silk. The report includes no evidence about which particles move.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Analyses the claim as incorrect, explaining that electrons move while protons stay in the nucleus, and linking the loss of electrons to the positive charge on the glass
4 marks: Analyses the claim as incorrect, stating clearly that electrons rather than protons move during rubbing
3 marks: Explains the movement of electrons during rubbing, without clearly judging whether the claim is correct
2 marks: Identifies that electrons are transferred during rubbing, with limited reference to the student's claim
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about charging by rubbing
markerNotes: Test the claim against the particle that actually moves, and say so explicitly.
Protons stay in the nucleus during rubbing, so the claim has to be rejected for this reason.
Link the loss of electrons to the sign of charge on each object, and show that total charge is conserved.
commonStudentErrors: Accepts the claim because the glass is positive, without checking which particle moved.
States that protons are rubbed off the glass, which confuses charging with a change in the nucleus.
Says the silk also becomes positive, which breaks conservation of charge.

sampleAnswers.answer: The claim is incorrect. Protons are held tightly in the nucleus and are not removed by rubbing, so they cannot move from the glass to the silk. The movement of electrons is what causes the charging, because electrons are loosely held in the outer shells and transfer between the two materials. The glass loses electrons to the silk, so it has fewer electrons than protons and has a net positive charge. The silk gains those electrons and becomes negatively charged. The charge gained by the silk equals the charge lost by the glass, which is conservation of charge. The student has the correct sign on the glass but has named the wrong particle.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5-mark row: the claim is judged incorrect, electron movement is explained, protons are excluded with reasons, and the charges are conserved.

sampleAnswers.answer: Electrons move from the glass to the silk during rubbing, leaving the glass with fewer electrons than protons. The glass therefore becomes positive and the silk becomes negative.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by explaining the movement of electrons and the resulting positive charge, but it does not judge the claim. Judging the claim as incorrect, with the reason that protons stay in the nucleus, would move it up to the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The glass and the silk become charged when they are rubbed together.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by giving relevant information about charging, but it identifies no particles and does not address the claim. Explaining which particles move would lift it to the 2-mark row.

dotPoints.description: Explain how friction, induction and conduction can cause objects to become electrically charged

prompts.question: Outline how induction can give an uncharged metal sphere a net positive charge, without the negative rod touching the sphere.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A negatively charged plastic rod is held close to, but not touching, an uncharged metal sphere on an insulating stand. While the rod stays in place, a student connects the sphere to earth with a wire, removes the wire, and then removes the rod.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Outlines the repulsion of electrons, the earthing step and the removal of the earth connection, and explains why the sphere is left positively charged without contact
2 marks: Outlines the repulsion of electrons in the sphere during induction, without explaining the earthing step or the final charge
1 mark: Identifies that induction charges an object without the objects touching
markerNotes: Set out the steps in order: electrons are repelled, the earth connection is made, the earth connection is removed, and then the rod is removed.
The sign of the final charge depends on which electrons leave, so state the direction of electron flow.
Use the contrast with friction and conduction to show why induction needs no contact.
commonStudentErrors: Says the sphere becomes negative because the rod was negative, which confuses induction with conduction.
Omits the removal of the earth connection before the rod, so the sphere is described as neutral.
States that the rod transfers electrons to the sphere by touching it, which contradicts the scenario.

sampleAnswers.answer: Unlike friction and conduction, induction charges the sphere electrically without any contact. The negative rod repels electrons in the sphere, so electrons move to the far side. When the sphere is earthed, electrons flow to earth. Removing the earth connection traps a shortage of electrons while the rod is still in place, so after the rod is removed the sphere is electrically charged, with a net positive charge.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row: the repulsion, the earthing step and the removal of the earth connection are all outlined, and the positive charge is explained.

sampleAnswers.answer: The negative rod repels electrons in the metal sphere, so electrons move to the far side. The sphere is then charged by induction, without the rod touching it.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by outlining the repulsion of electrons, but it does not explain the earthing step or the final positive charge. Adding the earth connection and its removal would lift it to the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Induction charges an object without the objects touching.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by identifying that contact is not needed, but it does not describe electron movement or the final charge. Outlining the repulsion of electrons would lift it to the 2-mark row.

prompts.question: Distinguish between charging by conduction and charging by induction, including the sign of the final charge in each case.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student charges a plastic rod negatively by friction with a cloth. The student then uses the rod in two experiments with identical neutral metal spheres. In experiment 1 the rod touches one sphere. In experiment 2 the rod is held close to, but not touching, a second sphere, which is earthed, the earth connection is removed, and then the rod is taken away.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Distinguishes conduction from induction by contact and by the sign of the final charge, with clear reasoning for both methods
4 marks: Distinguishes conduction from induction by contact or sign, with correct reasoning for one method and a gap in the other
3 marks: Describes how conduction and induction each charge a sphere, without explicitly distinguishing the two methods
2 marks: Identifies conduction, induction or friction as a way of charging an object, with limited explanation
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about charging an object
markerNotes: Distinguish using two criteria, contact and the sign of the final charge, and state both for each method.
Earthing lets induction leave a net charge after the rod is removed, so the earth step must be included.
Friction charges the rod, not the spheres, so keep the methods of charging each object separate.
commonStudentErrors: Says induction gives the same sign as the charging rod, which is the result of conduction.
Says induction needs the rod to touch the sphere, which contradicts the method.
Omits the removal of the earth connection before the rod is taken away.

sampleAnswers.answer: Conduction requires contact between the charged rod and the sphere. In experiment 1, electrons move from the negative rod onto the sphere, so the sphere is left with the same negative sign as the rod. Induction does not require contact. In experiment 2, the negative rod repels electrons in the second sphere, earthing lets electrons leave, and removing the earth connection and then the rod leaves the sphere electrically charged positive. Friction charged only the rod by moving electrons onto it, so it is not used to charge the spheres. The final sign therefore differs: conduction gives the same sign as the charging body, whereas induction gives the opposite sign.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5-mark row: contact is used to distinguish the methods, the sign of the final charge is correct for both, and the earth step is explained.

sampleAnswers.answer: In conduction, the rod touches the sphere and electrons move onto it, so the sphere becomes negative. In induction, the rod is held near the sphere, and the sphere is then charged by earthing it and removing the earth connection.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by describing how each method charges a sphere, but it never contrasts contact with the sign of the final charge. Stating that induction gives the opposite sign would move it to the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Charging can happen by friction, conduction or induction.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by naming methods of charging, but it does not explain or distinguish them. Describing how conduction works would lift it to the 2-mark row.

dotPoints.description: Outline characteristics of an electric field surrounding a point charge

prompts.question: Outline the characteristics of the electric field surrounding an isolated positive point charge.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A small sphere carrying a positive charge is suspended in an empty laboratory, far from other charged objects. A student wants to describe the electric field produced by the sphere, treating it as a point charge.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Outlines three characteristics of the field, including its radial direction, outward field lines and decreasing strength with distance
2 marks: Outlines two characteristics of the electric field around a positive point charge, with limited detail
1 mark: Identifies one characteristic of an electric field around a point charge
markerNotes: List three distinct characteristics, not one idea repeated in different words.
Include both the direction of the field and how its strength changes with distance.
State that the field points outward for a positive charge, not inward.
commonStudentErrors: States that the field points towards a positive point charge.
Describes the field as the same strength at every distance from the charge.
Gives only the shape of the field and no other characteristic.

sampleAnswers.answer: The electric field around a positive point charge is radial, so it points outward from the charge in all directions. Its field lines spread out evenly from the charge, and the field strength is greatest close to the charge. As distance increases, the field lines become further apart and the field strength decreases. A positive test charge placed in the field would be repelled along a field line.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row: the radial direction, the outward field lines and the decreasing strength are all outlined accurately.

sampleAnswers.answer: The field points outward from a positive point charge. Its strength is greatest near the charge and falls off with distance.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by outlining the outward direction and the falling strength, but the radial pattern is not named. Adding that the field is radial would lift it to the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The electric field points outward from the positive point charge.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by identifying the outward direction, but it does not describe how the strength changes. Adding how the strength changes with distance would lift it to the 2-mark row.

prompts.question: Analyse the student's claim that the electric field around a point charge has the same strength at every distance from the charge.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student draws several straight field lines radiating from a positive point charge. The student concludes that, because the field lines are straight, the field strength must be the same at every distance from the charge.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Analyses the claim as false, explaining that field strength falls with distance as the field lines spread out over a larger area
4 marks: Analyses the claim as false, with reference to the decrease in field strength with distance from the point charge
3 marks: Explains how the field strength of a point charge changes with distance, without clearly judging the claim
2 marks: Identifies that the electric field around a point charge is radial, with limited reference to strength
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about electric fields
markerNotes: Judge the claim directly, because the question asks for analysis and not only a description of the field.
Separate the direction of the field, which is radial, from its strength, which changes with distance.
Tie the strength to the spacing of the field lines, which is wider further from the charge.
commonStudentErrors: Says the field is uniform around a point charge because the field lines are straight.
Describes the field as getting stronger with distance, which reverses the relationship.
Confuses the direction of the field with its strength.

sampleAnswers.answer: The claim is incorrect. The electric field around a point charge is radial, so its field lines spread outward from the charge in every direction. At greater distance the same field lines are spread over a larger surface, so the lines become further apart and the field strength decreases. The field is therefore strongest close to the charge and weakest far from it. A constant field strength, or uniform field, is only found between large parallel charged plates, not around a point charge. Straight field lines show direction, not strength, and the spacing of the lines shows how strong the field is. The student has confused the direction of the field with its magnitude.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5-mark row: the claim is judged false with reasons, the falling strength is linked to the spacing of the field lines, and direction is separated from magnitude.

sampleAnswers.answer: The field around a point charge is radial, and field lines spread out from the charge. As the distance from the charge increases, the field lines are further apart and the field strength is smaller.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by explaining how the strength changes with distance, but it does not judge the claim. Stating that the claim is false would move it to the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The field around a point charge is an electric field produced by the charge.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by giving relevant information about electric fields, but it does not address the claim or the strength of the field. Describing the radial pattern would lift it to the 2-mark row.

dotPoints.description: Explain the role of static electricity in producing a lightning strike

prompts.question: Describe how static electricity builds up within a storm cloud before a lightning strike.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: Ice particles and water droplets move about inside a large storm cloud. The base of the cloud is observed to be negatively charged, and the ground beneath it becomes positively charged.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Describes how collisions separate charge within the storm cloud, building a strong electric field before the discharge
2 marks: Describes how static electricity builds up in the cloud, with some reference to charge separation
1 mark: Identifies that a lightning strike involves static electricity
markerNotes: Describe the charge separation caused by collisions, then state the resulting charges on the cloud and the ground.
Name the electric field as the link between separated charge and the discharge.
Say that the discharge happens when the field is strong enough to break down the air.
commonStudentErrors: Says the cloud becomes positive and the ground negative, which reverses the typical storm pattern.
Describes lightning as static electricity without any description of charge separation.
States that the storm cloud creates electrons from nothing, with no transfer.

sampleAnswers.answer: Collisions between ice particles and water droplets inside the storm cloud transfer electrons. This charge separation makes the lower part of the cloud negatively charged and the ground beneath it positively charged. The resulting electric field between the cloud and the ground grows stronger over time. When the field becomes strong enough to break down the air, a sudden discharge of static electricity occurs as a lightning strike.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row: the charge separation, the electric field and the discharge are all described in order.

sampleAnswers.answer: Ice particles and water droplets collide in the cloud, which separates charge. The lower cloud becomes negative, so static electricity builds up.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by describing charge separation, but it does not mention the electric field or the discharge. Explaining the field between cloud and ground would lift it to the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: A lightning strike is a discharge of static electricity.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by identifying static electricity as part of a lightning strike, but it does not describe how the charge builds up. Describing the charge separation would lift it to the 2-mark row.

prompts.question: Discuss why a lightning strike is more likely to hit the tall pointed flagpole than the low flat concrete slab, in terms of static electricity and the electric field.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A storm cloud has a negatively charged base, and the ground below it is positively charged. A tall metal flagpole with a sharp, pointed tip stands a short distance from a low, flat concrete slab.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Discusses how a stronger electric field near the tall pointed flagpole, produced by static electricity and a shorter distance to the cloud, makes a discharge path more likely
4 marks: Discusses the role of the electric field and static electricity in the strike location, with some reasoning about distance or shape
3 marks: Explains that the flagpole is closer to the charged cloud, without linking this to the electric field
2 marks: Identifies that static electricity builds up in the cloud, with limited link to the flagpole
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about lightning strikes
markerNotes: Explain the role of static electricity, not just the fact that lightning occurs.
Link distance and shape to the strength of the electric field, since the question asks for a discussion.
State where the electric field is strongest, and why that location is the likely discharge path.
commonStudentErrors: Says lightning strikes the tallest object because it is the most attractive, without any physics.
States that the field is strong everywhere between cloud and ground, with no comparison of the flagpole and the slab.
Describes the cloud base as positive, which reverses the charge in a typical storm cloud.

sampleAnswers.answer: The flagpole is more likely to be struck because of how static electricity and the electric field are concentrated there. The negatively charged base of the cloud induces a positive charge on the ground below it, and the electric field between cloud and ground is strongest where the distance is smallest. The tall flagpole reduces the distance to the cloud, so the air near its top experiences a stronger electric field than the air above the flat slab. Charge also collects on the pointed tip, which further strengthens the local electric field and makes the air easier to break down. Once the field is strong enough, the discharge follows the path through the tip, so a lightning strike is more likely to hit the flagpole than the slab.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5-mark row: the shorter distance and the pointed tip are linked to a stronger electric field caused by static electricity, which makes a discharge path more likely.

sampleAnswers.answer: The flagpole is taller, so it is closer to the negatively charged cloud base than the slab is. This makes a strike more likely to hit the flagpole.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by explaining the shorter distance to the cloud, but it does not connect this to the strength of the electric field. Adding that charge concentrates on the pointed tip would move it up to the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Lightning strikes are caused by static electricity in storm clouds.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by giving relevant information about lightning, but it does not compare the flagpole and the slab. Explaining why the flagpole is closer to the cloud would lift it to the 3-mark row.

prompts.question: Describe the electric field between a positive and a negative point charge, using field line diagrams.

Describe the spacing, showing where the field is stronger.
