dotPoints.description: Explain how the components of an AC induction motor are designed to support its function and operation

prompts.question: OUTLINE the roles of the stator and the rotor cage in turning the saw blade.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A workshop bench saw is driven by an AC induction motor. The motor has no brushes or commutator, and its rotor is a cage of metal bars joined at each end by a ring.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Outlines the stator as the source of a rotating magnetic field, and the rotor cage as the part where currents are induced, which turns the rotor
2 marks: Outlines the role of the stator or the rotor cage, with some accurate detail
1 mark: Identifies the stator or the rotor as a part of the motor
markerNotes: Give the stator its job: its coils, fed by AC, produce the rotating magnetic field.
For the rotor, say that currents are induced in the bars, rather than that the rotor is simply pushed.
Mention what is absent, such as brushes, when it helps explain why the motor is robust.
commonStudentErrors: Says the rotor is connected to the supply through brushes, which this motor does not have.
Describes the stator as the part that spins, when it is the fixed part.
Says the rotor is powered directly by the supply, when its current is induced.

sampleAnswers.answer: The stator is fed by the AC supply, and its coils produce a rotating magnetic field. The rotor cage is made of conducting bars joined by end rings. The rotating field induces currents in these bars, and the forces on those currents turn the rotor and the saw blade. The AC induction motor has no brushes or commutator, so no electrical contact is needed to the rotor.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by outlining the rotating field from the stator and the induced currents that turn the rotor. The middle answer describes the parts in general terms, without the field or the induced currents.

sampleAnswers.answer: The stator is the fixed part with coils, and the rotor is the part that spins inside it.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by outlining the stator and rotor in general terms. It does not explain the rotating magnetic field or the induced currents.

sampleAnswers.answer: The motor has a stator and a rotor.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by identifying the parts. It gives no role for either one.

prompts.question: DISCUSS how the components of the AC induction motor are designed to support its function and operation in this application, and the points the manager should weigh up.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A factory manager is choosing between an AC induction motor and a DC motor with brushes and a commutator to drive a continuous conveyor belt. The manager is concerned about maintenance and the cost of replacing worn parts.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Discusses how the components of the AC induction motor support its function and operation, and weighs up the advantages against the limitations for the conveyor belt
5 marks: Discusses the components and operation of the AC induction motor with relevant detail, and identifies both an advantage and a limitation
4 marks: Describes the design of the components and their function with some relevant detail, without weighing up the trade-offs
3 marks: Describes one feature of the motor and its role in its operation, with limited reference to the application
2 marks: Identifies a feature of the AC induction motor, with minimal explanation
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about electric motors
markerNotes: Tie each design feature, such as the rotor cage or the lack of brushes, to a specific function or operation.
Weigh up both sides: the advantages for this belt and the limitations, such as speed control and starting current.
Refer back to the manager's concerns about maintenance, so the discussion stays on the application.
commonStudentErrors: Lists features of the motor without saying how any of them supports its function.
Argues only for the AC induction motor and never gives a limitation, so the discussion is one-sided.
Says the AC induction motor needs brushes to transfer current to the rotor.

sampleAnswers.answer: The AC induction motor suits a conveyor belt because its components are designed for reliable, continuous operation. The stator coils are fed by the AC supply and produce a rotating magnetic field, and the rotor is a cage of conducting bars. The rotating field induces currents in these bars, and the forces on those currents turn the rotor and the belt. Because the motor has no brushes or commutator, there are fewer parts to wear and spark, so it needs less maintenance than a DC motor. Laminated iron cores reduce eddy currents and concentrate the magnetic flux, which supports the motor's function. The manager should weigh these strengths against the limitations: speed control is less simple than in a DC motor and usually needs an electronic drive, and the starting current is high.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row by showing how the components support the motor's function and operation, and weighing the advantages against the limitations for the belt. The middle answer describes the design but does not weigh up the trade-offs.

sampleAnswers.answer: The AC induction motor has a stator with coils that produce a rotating magnetic field, and a rotor that turns in response. It has no brushes, so there is less wear than in a DC motor, which suits a conveyor belt.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-mark row by describing the design of the components and their function with some relevant detail. It does not weigh up the trade-offs, so it cannot reach the 5-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: An AC induction motor is reliable, so the manager may want to buy one.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by identifying one feature of the motor with minimal explanation. It does not refer to any component.

dotPoints.description: Explain how electromagnetic induction causes a torque on the armature of a brushless DC motor

prompts.question: DESCRIBE how the rotating permanent magnets induce an emf in the armature windings, and what this induced emf opposes.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A small drone uses a brushless DC motor to turn its propeller. The motor has permanent magnets on its rotor and a set of armature windings, and an electronic controller switches current through the windings in sequence.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Describes the changing magnetic flux through the armature windings as the magnets turn, and states that the induced emf opposes the supply voltage
2 marks: Describes the changing magnetic flux through the armature windings as the magnets turn, without stating what the induced emf opposes
1 mark: Identifies that the motor's magnets and windings interact to produce a voltage
markerNotes: Name the process as electromagnetic induction, and link it to the changing flux rather than to the magnets alone.
State that the induced emf opposes the supply, which is Lenz's law at work.
Refer to the coils as armature windings, since they are the parts that carry the current.
commonStudentErrors: Says the magnets produce an emf directly, without a changing magnetic flux through the windings.
Says the induced emf adds to the supply voltage, when it opposes it.
Describes the magnets turning without linking this to the windings.

sampleAnswers.answer: In this brushless DC motor, the rotating permanent magnets change the magnetic flux through the armature windings. This is electromagnetic induction: the changing flux induces an emf in the windings. By Lenz's law, the induced emf opposes the change that produces it, so it acts against the supply voltage that drives the current. This induced emf is the back emf of the motor.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by describing the changing flux through the armature windings and stating that the induced emf opposes the supply. The middle answer describes the changing flux but does not say what the emf opposes.

sampleAnswers.answer: As the magnets turn, the magnetic flux through the armature windings changes, which induces a voltage in the windings.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by describing the changing flux that induces a voltage. It does not say what the induced emf opposes, so it cannot reach the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The motor uses electromagnetic induction, so its magnets and windings interact.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by identifying an interaction between the magnets and windings. It does not describe the changing flux.

prompts.question: JUSTIFY whether the student's claim is correct, referring to the current in the armature windings and to electromagnetic induction.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student claims that the torque on the armature of a brushless DC motor is produced directly by the induced emf, so a stronger induced emf always gives a larger torque. The student's reasoning ignores the role of the current.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Justifies that the claim is incorrect, explaining that torque depends on the current in the armature windings, while the induced emf depends on speed and sets the power
5 marks: Justifies that the claim is incorrect, with a sound explanation of the force on the current in the armature windings
4 marks: Explains that torque depends on the current in the armature, with some reasoning about the induced emf
3 marks: Describes the armature and the induced emf, with limited reasoning about the torque
2 marks: Identifies a relationship between the induced emf and the torque, with minimal reasoning
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about brushless DC motors
markerNotes: State that the claim is incorrect in the opening sentence, then support it with the force on the current.
Link the induced emf to speed and power, not to torque directly.
Name electromagnetic induction as the cause of the back emf, so the link to the motor's operation is clear.
commonStudentErrors: Says torque is the induced emf, so a larger emf always gives a larger torque.
Describes the force on the armature without saying what the current depends on.
Says the back emf adds to the supply, when it opposes it.

sampleAnswers.answer: The claim is incorrect. In this brushless DC motor, the torque on the armature comes from the force on the current in the armature windings when they sit in the magnetic field of the rotor magnets, so it depends on the current rather than directly on the induced emf. The rotating magnets change the flux through the windings, and by electromagnetic induction this produces a back emf that opposes the supply. This back emf grows with the speed of the rotor and limits the current the controller can drive through the windings. The power converted to mechanical energy is the back emf times the current, so for a given current the torque is unchanged even when the induced emf is larger at higher speed. The student has confused a larger induced emf with a larger torque: the torque is set by the current, and the induced emf sets how much power that current can deliver.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row by justifying that the claim is incorrect, with torque tied to the current and the induced emf tied to speed and power. The middle answer gets the force-on-current idea but does not link the induced emf to power.

sampleAnswers.answer: The torque comes from the force on the current in the armature windings, so it depends on the current. A larger induced emf does not automatically give a bigger torque.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-mark row by explaining that torque depends on the current, with some reasoning about the induced emf. It does not describe electromagnetic induction or the back emf, and it does not link power and speed.

sampleAnswers.answer: Torque and induced emf are both produced in the armature when the motor runs, so they are linked.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by identifying a link between the induced emf and the torque, with minimal reasoning. It does not explain how the link works.

dotPoints.description: Explain how a force opposing motion is generated during electromagnetic braking

prompts.question: Explain these observations.
markerNotes: Link each balance reading to a stage of the motion: the rise while the magnet speeds up, and the constant maximum at steady speed.
Name the force on the pipe as the reaction to the upward force on the magnet.
Explain the currents: the changing flux induces eddy currents in the copper, which oppose the fall.
commonStudentErrors: Says the reading rises because the magnet gets heavier as it falls.
Describes the eddy currents without saying how their force reaches the balance.
Says the force on the pipe is upward, so the reading falls.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Relates the measurements on the balance to the motion of the magnet and its interactions with the pipe
3 marks: Relates a measurement on the balance to the motion of the magnet and aspects of its interactions with the pipe
2 marks: Describes some aspects of the motion of the magnet and relates this to a measurement on the balance; OR; Describes the motion of the magnet and/or interactions with the pipe
1 mark: Provides some relevant information

sampleAnswers.answer:
The reading on the scale has two phases.
1. The magnet accelerates to a maximum speed. This results in an increasing change in magnetic flux causing the creation of an increasing electromagnetic force that opposes the constant gravitational force acting on the magnet. The force on the magnet due to this interaction produces an equal and opposite force on the pipe, which results in an increase in the downward force on the scale.
2. The magnet reaches a constant speed when the upward electromagnetic force is equal and opposite to the weight force of the magnet. The force of the magnet on the pipe will be equal to the weight of the magnet. The reading on the scale will then be the weight of the pipe and magnet, shown in grams.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-mark row by linking the balance readings to the induced current in the pipe, the opposing force on the magnet, its reaction on the pipe, and the constant reading once the forces balance. The middle answer describes the falling magnet and its interaction with the pipe, but does not link these to the balance.

sampleAnswers.answer: As the magnet falls, the changing magnetic field induces currents in the copper pipe. These currents push back on the magnet, so it accelerates more slowly than it would in free fall. At first the magnet speeds up, then it reaches a steady speed while still inside the pipe.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by describing the magnet’s motion and its interaction with the pipe: “currents push back on the magnet”. It does not link either to the balance reading. Relating the extra downward force on the pipe to the rise in the reading would lift it to the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Copper is a good conductor of current.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by giving relevant information about copper, but it does not describe the motion or any force. Describing the induced current as opposing the magnet's fall would lift it to the 2-mark row.

dotPoints.description: Outline the differences between a motor and a generator in terms of energy transformation

prompts.question: OUTLINE the energy transformations in the desk fan and in the hand-cranked torch.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A desk fan is driven by an electric motor, and a hand-cranked torch is powered by a generator. In the torch, the user turns a handle that spins a coil between magnets, and the coil feeds a bulb.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Outlines the electrical-to-kinetic transformation in the fan and the kinetic-to-electrical transformation in the torch, and notes the energy lost as heat in each
2 marks: Outlines the energy transformation in one device, or identifies the input and output energy of both devices
1 mark: Identifies that the devices transform energy between electrical and kinetic forms
markerNotes: Name the energy form at the input and the output of each device, rather than saying that energy is used.
Mention the heat losses so that each transformation is complete.
Keep the two devices separate and show the direction of energy in each.
commonStudentErrors: Says the motor produces electrical energy from the fan's blades.
Says the energy is used up, without naming the form it becomes.
Describes only the useful output and never mentions heat lost in either device.

sampleAnswers.answer: The desk fan's motor makes an energy transformation from electrical energy to the kinetic energy of the rotating blades, and some electrical energy is also lost as heat in the coils and bearings. In the torch, the generator makes the opposite energy transformation: the kinetic energy of the turning handle becomes electrical energy, which lights the bulb. Some of this kinetic energy is also lost as heat, so the bulb receives less energy than the handle supplies.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by outlining both transformations and noting the heat lost in each. The middle answer identifies the input and output energy of both devices but does not mention the heat losses.

sampleAnswers.answer: The fan's motor changes electrical energy into kinetic energy. The torch's generator changes kinetic energy into electrical energy.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by identifying the input and output energy of both devices. It does not mention energy lost as heat, so it cannot reach the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The fan and the torch both use energy in different forms.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by giving relevant information about energy forms. It does not show either transformation.

prompts.question: DISTINGUISH between the energy transformations in a motor and in a generator, to test the student's claim.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student claims that a motor and a generator convert energy in the same direction, because both use a coil and magnets in the same way. The student's reasoning does not consider which way the energy flows.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Distinguishes the energy transformations of the motor and the generator, showing they run in opposite directions, and explains that the same coil and magnet arrangement can operate in either role
4 marks: Distinguishes the energy transformations of the motor and the generator, showing that the energy flows in opposite directions
3 marks: Describes the energy transformation in the motor and in the generator, with limited comparison of their directions
2 marks: Identifies one energy transformation in either the motor or the generator
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about motors or generators
markerNotes: State the input and output of each device, then show that the two are reversed.
Acknowledge what the student gets right, the shared construction, before correcting the direction.
Mention the heat losses in each transformation, so the energy account is complete.
commonStudentErrors: Says a generator turns electrical energy into kinetic energy, which is the motor's transformation.
Says the student is right because the coil and magnets are the same in both devices.
Describes the motor only and never gives the generator's transformation.

sampleAnswers.answer: A motor transforms electrical energy into kinetic energy: the electrical input drives a current through the coil, and the magnetic forces from the magnets on the coil turn the shaft. A generator does the reverse: the kinetic energy of the turning shaft moves the coil through the magnetic field of the magnets, and the generator transforms this into electrical energy. In each case the energy transformation is not perfect, and some energy is lost as heat in the coil and bearings. The student is right that the same coil and magnet arrangement can work in either role, but the direction of the energy transformation is opposite. The motor's input is electrical and its output is kinetic, while the generator's input is kinetic and its output is electrical.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5-mark row by distinguishing the two transformations, showing they run in opposite directions, and explaining the shared construction. The middle answer describes each device without comparing the directions.

sampleAnswers.answer: A motor uses electrical energy to make things move, and a generator makes electrical energy from movement. Both devices involve coils and magnets.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by describing the transformation in each device, with little comparison of their directions. It does not show that the energy flows in opposite directions, so it cannot reach the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Motors and generators both contain coils and magnets.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by giving relevant information about the devices. It does not describe either energy transformation.

dotPoints.description: Explain the production of back emf in simple DC motors

prompts.question: DESCRIBE how the rotating coil produces a voltage that acts against the battery voltage.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student connects a simple DC motor to a battery. The motor's coil begins to rotate in the magnetic field of the motor's permanent magnets as soon as the switch is closed.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Describes the changing magnetic flux through the rotating coil, and explains that the induced voltage opposes the battery voltage
2 marks: Describes the changing magnetic flux through the rotating coil, without stating how the induced voltage acts on the supply
1 mark: Identifies that the rotating coil produces a voltage in the motor
markerNotes: Describe the changing flux as the cause, then say that the induced voltage opposes the battery.
Name the voltage as back emf, the term used for a motor.
Cite Lenz's law as the reason the induced voltage opposes the change that produces it.
commonStudentErrors: Says the battery produces the back emf, rather than the rotating coil.
Says the back emf adds to the battery voltage.
Describes the coil rotating without linking the rotation to a changing magnetic flux.

sampleAnswers.answer: As the coil rotates, the magnetic flux through it changes, and this induces a voltage in the coil by electromagnetic induction. By Lenz's law, the induced voltage opposes the change that produces it, so it acts against the battery voltage. This induced voltage is the back emf of the DC motor, and it reduces the net voltage that drives the current through the coil.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by describing the changing flux and stating that the induced voltage opposes the battery voltage. The middle answer describes the changing flux without saying how the voltage acts on the supply.

sampleAnswers.answer: The coil turns in a magnetic field, so the flux through it changes and a voltage is induced in the coil.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by describing the changing flux that induces the voltage. It does not say how the voltage acts on the battery, so it cannot reach the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The motor has a coil that produces a voltage when it spins.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by identifying a voltage from the rotating coil. It gives no cause and no effect on the battery voltage.

prompts.question: ASSESS the student's claim, referring to what determines the size of the back emf.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student claims that a simple DC motor has its largest back emf at the moment it is first switched on, because the current is greatest at that moment. The motor is supplied from a battery that gives a fixed voltage.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Assesses the claim as incorrect, explaining that back emf is zero at start and grows with speed, and identifies the factors that set its size
5 marks: Assesses the claim as incorrect, explaining that back emf grows with the rotational speed of the coil, with sound reference to the current
4 marks: Explains that back emf depends on the speed of the coil and that the current is largest at start, with some judgement of the claim
3 marks: Describes how the back emf changes as the motor speeds up, with limited reference to the student's claim
2 marks: Identifies that back emf is related to the speed of the motor, with minimal reasoning
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about back emf in DC motors
markerNotes: Test the claim against the physics: back emf depends on speed, so it is zero at the moment of switch-on.
Say that the largest current and the largest back emf occur at opposite times, which shows the link.
Name the factors that set the back emf: speed, magnetic field strength and number of turns on the coil.
commonStudentErrors: Says back emf is largest at start because the current is largest then, which reverses cause and effect.
Treats back emf as fixed, rather than a value that changes with the speed of the motor.
Says the back emf is zero at all times, which contradicts the voltage induced in the rotating coil.

sampleAnswers.answer: The student's claim is incorrect. At the moment of switch-on, the coil is stationary, so the magnetic flux through it is not changing and there is no back emf to oppose the battery. The current is greatest at this instant only because nothing opposes the battery voltage, so the coil's resistance is the only limit. As the coil speeds up, the flux changes more rapidly, and by electromagnetic induction the back emf grows in proportion to the speed of rotation. The back emf therefore depends on the speed, on the strength of the magnetic field and on the number of turns on the coil. It is largest when the DC motor reaches its steady top speed, and at that point the current is at its smallest, so the largest back emf and the largest current occur at opposite times.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row by assessing the claim as incorrect, explaining that back emf is zero at start and grows with speed, and naming the factors that set its size. The middle answer judges the claim but does not name the factors.

sampleAnswers.answer: The back emf is zero when the motor starts, so the claim has the cause and effect the wrong way round. It increases as the motor speeds up, and the current is greatest at start because the back emf is smallest then.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-mark row by explaining that back emf depends on the speed of the coil, that the current is largest at start, and judging the claim. It does not name the factors that set the size of the back emf.

sampleAnswers.answer: Back emf is related to the speed of the motor, but the answer does not say whether the claim is correct.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by identifying a link between back emf and speed, with minimal reasoning. It does not assess the claim.

dotPoints.description: Explain the effects of back emf on the current flowing through and speed of a simple DC motor

prompts.question: PREDICT how the current drawn by the motor changes after the load is attached, and why.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A simple DC motor runs at a steady speed with no load on its shaft. A load is then attached to the shaft, and the motor's speed falls.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Predicts that the current increases, and explains that the lower speed reduces the back emf, so the net voltage driving the current rises
2 marks: Predicts that the current increases, with a reason that refers to the back emf only in general terms
1 mark: Identifies that the load affects the current drawn by the motor
markerNotes: Give the direction first, then the chain: lower speed, lower back emf, higher net voltage, higher current.
Name the back emf as the quantity that falls, not the supply voltage.
Tie the change to the load, which is the cause of the slowing.
commonStudentErrors: Says the current falls because the motor is working harder.
Says the back emf rises when the motor slows, which reverses the effect.
Predicts the current increases but gives no link to the back emf.

sampleAnswers.answer: The current increases. When the load slows the motor, the speed of the coil falls, so the flux through it changes more slowly and the back emf falls. The back emf opposes the supply voltage, so as it falls the net voltage across the coil rises, and a larger current flows. The simple DC motor therefore draws more current when it is loaded than when it runs freely.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by predicting the increase and explaining that the lower speed reduces the back emf and raises the net voltage. The middle answer predicts the increase with a general reason about the back emf.

sampleAnswers.answer: The current goes up because the motor is slowing down and its back emf is lower.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by predicting the increase with a reason about the back emf, in general terms. It does not explain how the net voltage changes, so it cannot reach the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The load makes the motor work harder, which changes the current.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by identifying that the load affects the current. It gives no direction and no reason.

prompts.question: ANALYSE why the motor's speed settles at a value where the back emf is almost equal to the supply voltage, and what this means for the current drawn.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A simple DC motor is connected to a supply with no load on its shaft. After starting, it settles at a steady speed.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Analyses the balance between the back emf and the supply voltage, explaining that the net voltage and current fall to small values as the speed rises to its steady value
5 marks: Analyses the balance between the back emf and the supply voltage, with sound reference to the current that remains at steady speed
4 marks: Explains the effect of back emf on the current and the steady speed, with some analysis of the balance of voltages
3 marks: Describes the back emf as the motor speeds up, with limited reference to the current or the steady speed
2 marks: Identifies a link between the speed of the motor and the current drawn, with minimal explanation
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about back emf or DC motors
markerNotes: Describe the balance as voltages: the supply voltage is shared between the back emf and the voltage needed to drive the current through the coil.
Explain the start: zero back emf gives the largest current, which falls as the speed builds.
Say what a load does to the steady speed, to show the link between load, back emf and current.
commonStudentErrors: Says the back emf is larger than the supply voltage at steady speed, which would reverse the current.
Says the current stays the same as the speed increases, without connecting it to the back emf.
Says the speed stops rising because the back emf reaches zero.

sampleAnswers.answer: The motor speeds up until the back emf is almost equal to the supply voltage. While the DC motor is at rest, the back emf is zero, so the full supply voltage drives a large current through the coil. As the coil turns, the flux through it changes and induces a back emf that opposes the supply, reducing the net voltage across the coil. The current therefore falls as the speed rises. With no load, the motor settles at the steady speed where the net voltage is just large enough to supply the small current needed to overcome friction and heat losses. At this steady speed the back emf is close to the supply voltage, so the current is small. If a load is added, the speed falls, the back emf falls and the current rises to supply the extra torque.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row by analysing the balance of back emf and supply voltage, and showing how the current falls to a small value at steady speed and rises under load. The middle answer explains the effect of back emf but does not describe the start-up.

sampleAnswers.answer: As the motor speeds up, the back emf increases and the current falls. At the steady speed, the back emf is close to the supply voltage, so the current is small.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-mark row by explaining the effect of back emf on the current and the steady speed. It does not analyse the balance of voltages in full, so it cannot reach the 5-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The motor speeds up until it reaches a steady speed, and the current changes.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by identifying a link between speed and current. It gives no reason for the change and does not mention back emf.

dotPoints.description: Outline the structure and function of components in a simple AC generator and a simple DC generator, including rotor coils, stator magnets, brushes, and slip rings and split-ring commutators

prompts.question: OUTLINE the function of the slip rings and brushes in generator X, and of the split-ring commutator and brushes in generator Y.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student builds two simple generators from the same rotor coil and stator magnets. Generator X has two continuous slip rings, and generator Y has a split-ring commutator. Both generators have brushes that press on their rings or commutator.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Outlines the role of the rotor coil, stator magnets, slip rings and brushes in generator X, and of the split-ring commutator in generator Y, with accurate detail
2 marks: Outlines the function of the slip rings or the split-ring commutator, with some accurate detail
1 mark: Identifies the brushes or the rotor coil as a component of a generator
markerNotes: Give each part a function: the coil and magnets produce the emf, while the rings or commutator and brushes deliver it.
Contrast the slip rings, which keep the connections fixed, with the split-ring commutator, which reverses them.
Name the brushes as the sliding contacts that carry current out of the moving coil.
commonStudentErrors: Says the slip rings reverse the connections every half turn, which is the commutator's job.
Says the brushes generate the current.
Describes the components without saying what each one does.

sampleAnswers.answer: In generator X, the rotor coil turns between the stator magnets, and its continuous slip rings keep the connections fixed. The brushes carry the induced current from the rings to the external circuit, so the output alternates. In generator Y, the split-ring commutator reverses the connections to the brushes every half turn, so the output keeps one direction. The brushes are sliding contacts that link the moving coil to the outside circuit.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by outlining the role of each component in both generators with accurate detail. The middle answer covers the rings and commutator but not the rotor coil or the brushes.

sampleAnswers.answer: The slip rings let the generator output an alternating current, and the split-ring commutator keeps the output in one direction.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by outlining the function of the slip rings and the commutator, with some accurate detail. It does not describe the rotor coil or the brushes, so it cannot reach the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The brushes are contacts that connect the coil to the outside circuit.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by identifying the brushes as a component. It gives no detail of how the rings or the commutator work.

prompts.question: ANALYSE how the worn brushes affect the current delivered to the lamp, identifying the roles of the rotor coil, stator magnets, slip rings and brushes in producing and delivering that current.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A hand-cranked AC generator with slip rings lights a lamp. After long use, the brushes wear and no longer press firmly on the slip rings, and the lamp begins to flicker.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Analyses how the worn brushes disrupt the current, explaining that the rotor coil and stator magnets still induce an emf while the faulty contact at the slip rings reduces and disturbs the delivered current
5 marks: Analyses the roles of the rotor coil, stator magnets, slip rings and brushes, and explains the effect of worn brushes on the current to the lamp
4 marks: Describes the roles of the components in producing and delivering current, and links the worn brushes to a reduced or uneven current
3 marks: Describes the roles of the brushes and slip rings in delivering current, with limited reference to the fault
2 marks: Identifies the effect of worn brushes on the lamp, with minimal reference to the components
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about generators or lamps
markerNotes: Separate the roles: the rotor coil and stator magnets make the emf, while the brushes and rings deliver it.
Link worn brushes to higher contact resistance and an uneven current, not just to a fault.
Say the emf is still produced, so the fault lies in the delivery path.
commonStudentErrors: Says the worn brushes stop the rotor coil from producing any emf.
Says the lamp flickers because the generator makes a steady current.
Blames the stator magnets for the fault without any link to the brushes.

sampleAnswers.answer: The rotor coil and the stator magnets produce the alternating emf: as the coil turns, the magnetic flux through it changes and an emf is induced. The slip rings and brushes carry this current out of the generator to the lamp. When the brushes wear, they no longer press firmly on the slip rings, so the contact resistance rises and the connection becomes intermittent. The current delivered to the lamp is therefore reduced and uneven, which is seen as flickering. The rotor coil and stator magnets still produce the same emf, so the fault lies in the brushes and their contact with the slip rings. Replacing or realigning the brushes restores a firm, low-resistance contact, and the current reaching the lamp becomes consistent again. The fault is therefore a failure of the components that deliver the current, not of the components that induce it.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row by separating the roles of the components, explaining how the worn brushes raise the contact resistance, and locating the fault in the delivery path. The middle answer describes the roles but does not explain the rise in contact resistance.

sampleAnswers.answer: The rotor coil turns in the magnetic field of the stator magnets, and the current reaches the lamp through the slip rings and brushes. If the brushes are worn, the current to the lamp is reduced.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-mark row by describing the roles of the components and linking the worn brushes to a reduced current. It does not explain the rise in contact resistance or why the lamp flickers.

sampleAnswers.answer: Worn brushes do not make good contact, so the lamp may flicker.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by identifying the effect of worn brushes on the lamp, with minimal reference to the components.

dotPoints.description: Explain the variations in current produced by AC generators and DC generators

prompts.question: DESCRIBE how the magnitude and direction of the current change over one complete rotation of the coil.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student turns the handle of a simple AC generator at a steady rate and watches a current-measuring device connected to its slip rings. The device shows the current through one full rotation of the coil.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Describes the current as reversing direction twice and varying in size in a sinusoidal pattern, linked to the changing rate of flux through the coil
2 marks: Describes the current as changing direction and size over one rotation, without linking this to the rate of change of flux
1 mark: Identifies that the current changes direction during one rotation
markerNotes: Describe both features: the direction reverses twice per rotation, and the size follows a sinusoidal pattern.
Link the pattern to the rate of change of flux, not just to the coil turning.
Say that the slip rings do not reverse, so the reversal comes from the induced emf.
commonStudentErrors: Says the current stays the same size because the coil turns at a steady rate.
Says the current reverses once every full rotation, instead of twice.
Describes the output of the AC generator as direct current.

sampleAnswers.answer: Over one complete rotation, the current from the AC generator reverses direction twice. Its magnitude rises from zero to a peak and falls back to zero in each half of the rotation, following a sinusoidal pattern. This happens because the induced emf depends on the rate of change of flux through the coil, which varies with the coil's angle. The slip rings keep their connections fixed, so the current in the external circuit reverses with the emf.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by describing the two reversals and the sinusoidal size pattern, linked to the rate of change of flux. The middle answer describes the changes without that link.

sampleAnswers.answer: The current changes direction during each rotation, and its size changes as the coil turns.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by describing the changing direction and size. It does not link the pattern to the rate of change of flux, so it cannot reach the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The current from an AC generator is alternating.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by identifying that the current changes direction. It does not describe its size or how it varies.

prompts.question: JUSTIFY whether the student's claim is correct, referring to how the size of the current from a simple DC generator varies over one rotation of the coil.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student says that the current from a simple DC generator is steady, because its direction never changes. The student's teacher disagrees with this conclusion.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Justifies that the claim is incorrect, explaining that the split-ring commutator keeps the direction constant while the emf and current rise and fall to zero each half turn
5 marks: Justifies that the claim is incorrect, with a sound explanation that the current varies in size even though its direction is constant
4 marks: Explains that the current keeps one direction but its size varies over the rotation, with some reasoning about the commutator
3 marks: Describes the constant direction of the current, with limited reference to how its size changes
2 marks: Identifies that the current from a DC generator does not change direction, without considering its size
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about DC generators or commutators
markerNotes: Acknowledge the correct part, the constant direction, before showing why the claim fails.
Use the emf pattern over one rotation as the evidence that the size is not steady.
Name the split-ring commutator as the reason the direction stays constant.
commonStudentErrors: Says a constant direction means a steady current, which confuses direction with size.
Says the current from a DC generator is alternating, which is the AC generator's output.
Describes the commutator without linking it to the direction of the current.

sampleAnswers.answer: The claim is only partly right. The direction of the current from a simple DC generator is constant, because the split-ring commutator reverses the connections to the external circuit each time the induced emf reverses. However, the current is not steady. The induced emf depends on the rate of change of flux through the coil, which varies with the coil's angle during each rotation. As the coil turns, the emf rises from zero to a peak and falls back to zero, and this happens twice per rotation. The commutator therefore produces pulses of current in one direction, with the size changing between zero and a maximum. A steady current would need a constant emf throughout the rotation, which does not occur. The claim that the current is steady is therefore incorrect.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row by justifying that the claim is incorrect, with the constant direction and the varying size both explained. The middle answer explains the constant direction and the pulsing size but does not refer to the emf over the rotation.

sampleAnswers.answer: The split-ring commutator keeps the current in one direction, but its size changes over each rotation, so the current is pulsing rather than steady.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-mark row by explaining that the direction is constant while the size varies, with some reasoning about the commutator. It does not refer to the emf over the rotation or fully justify the conclusion.

sampleAnswers.answer: The current from a DC generator always flows in the same direction.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by identifying the constant direction. It does not consider the size of the current, so it cannot judge the claim.

prompts.question: Using the particle model of light, explain the features shown in the experimental results.
markerNotes: Explain the rising stopping voltage: it measures the maximum kinetic energy of the electrons, which rises with frequency.
Link each feature in the data to a photon idea, such as E = hf or Kmax = hf − ϕ.
Use the work function, the energy needed to free an electron, to explain why electrons leave only above a threshold frequency.
commonStudentErrors: Describes the wave model, such as the amplitude of the light, instead of the particle model.
States that higher frequency means more intensity, without relating it to electron energy.
Says the stopping voltage is the energy of the photons.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Shows how the features shown in the experiment are explained by the particle model of light
2 marks: Relates a feature shown to an aspect of the particle model of light
1 mark: Provides some relevant information

sampleAnswers.answer:
The photon model of light explains the trend by stating that light consists of discrete packets of energy called photons. The energy of a photon is directly proportional to its frequency (E = hf). When photons strike the metal, they transfer energy to electrons. If the photon energy exceeds the work function of the metal, the threshold frequency is exceeded and electrons are ejected with kinetic energy proportional to the excess energy (KE = hf – ϕ).
As the frequency of light increases, the photon energy increases, resulting in higher kinetic energy for the ejected electrons. This is observed as a higher stopping voltage, which is required to halt the more energetic electrons.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row: the particle model explains the rising stopping voltage through E = hf and Kmax = hf − ϕ, and the work function sets the threshold. A middle answer links one feature to a photon idea without the kinetic energy link.

sampleAnswers.answer: In the photon model, light is made of discrete packets of energy called photons. The energy of each photon is E = hf, so higher frequency light has more energy per photon. When a photon strikes the potassium, it transfers its energy to a single electron, and the electron leaves the metal with more kinetic energy when the photon has more energy.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by relating the rise in frequency to photon energy, one aspect of the particle model: “energy of each photon is E = hf”. It does not link the kinetic energy to the stopping voltage or mention the work function. Adding KE = hf − ϕ, and that the stopping voltage measures this kinetic energy, would lift it to the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: In the particle model, light is a stream of photons.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by giving relevant information about the particle model, but it does not explain any feature in the data. Linking the photon energy to the electron energy would lift it to the 2-mark row.

prompts.question: Analyse the consequences of the theory of special relativity in relation to length, time and motion. Support your answer with reference to experimental evidence.
markerNotes: Analyse each consequence (time, length and motion) from the two postulates, not only define it.
Support at least one consequence with experimental evidence, such as the muon flux, and say what the evidence shows.
Name the frame of reference in each effect: who measures what.
commonStudentErrors: Lists time dilation and length contraction as definitions without linking them to the postulates.
Refers to the muon evidence without saying in which frame the effect is observed.
Says an object's mass increases with speed, rather than its relativistic momentum.
prompts.markingCriteria:
8 marks: Provides a comprehensive analysis of the consequences of special relativity on time, length and motion; Refers to applicable experimental evidence
6-7 marks: Provides a thorough analysis of the consequences of special relativity on time, length and motion; Refers to applicable experimental evidence
4-5 marks: Provides analysis of the consequences of special relativity on time and/or length and/or motion; Refers to some relevant experimental evidence
2-3 marks: Makes some reference to special relativity and/or related experimental evidence
1 mark: Provides some relevant information

sampleAnswers.answer:
The two postulates of special relativity are: the speed of light in a vacuum is an absolute constant, and all inertial frames of reference are equivalent.
The consequences of these postulates are time dilation, length contraction and relativistic momentum dilation. Time dilation means that the measured time between events increases as the speed of an observer increases. Length contraction means that the length of an object decreases as the speed of an observer increases, and relativistic momentum dilation means that objects (with mass) cannot travel at c as it takes increasing amounts of energy to accelerate objects as they approach the speed of light.
Length contraction and time dilation can both be seen in observations of muons at Earth’s surface. The short half-life of muons suggests that there should be very few of them that arrive at Earth’s surface from their point of origin high in Earth’s atmosphere, but the muon flux is greater than suggested by half-life and distance travelled alone. However, when the distance travelled is considered from the muon’s frame of reference, it is length-contracted according to l = l₀√(1 − v²/c²), giving an effective shorter distance for them to travel. From the perspective of an observer on Earth’s surface, the time taken for them to decay is dilated, giving an effective greater amount of time for them to travel before decaying.
The effects of relativistic momentum can be seen in particle accelerators in terms of the increasing amounts of energy to required to accelerate the particles as they approach the speed of light – it is though the objects are much more massive than they are.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 8-mark row: the postulates are used to analyse time dilation, length contraction and relativistic momentum for different observers, with muon and particle evidence. The middle answer analyses time and length with one piece of evidence but does not analyse motion.

sampleAnswers.answer: Special relativity rests on two postulates: the speed of light in a vacuum is the same for all observers, and the laws of physics are the same in all inertial frames. One consequence is time dilation. A moving clock runs slow when observed from a frame in which it moves, so the time between events is longer for that observer. Another is length contraction, in which a moving object is shorter along its direction of motion. Muons created high in the atmosphere reach the ground in greater numbers than their short half-life predicts, which is evidence for time dilation as seen from Earth.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5-mark row by analysing time dilation and length contraction from the postulates and supporting them with the muon evidence. It does not analyse the effect on motion or momentum, which the 6-7 row needs, so adding how the energy needed to accelerate an object grows as it nears c would lift it.

sampleAnswers.answer: Special relativity says the speed of light is the same for all observers, and that moving clocks run slow. Experiments with fast particles have confirmed time dilation.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-3 mark row by referring to special relativity and to related experimental evidence. It gives no analysis of time, length or motion, and explaining how the time interval changes for an observer would lift it to the 4-5 row.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Experimental results and their interpretation have played an essential role in developing and understanding of both the existence and properties of electrons.
It was demonstrated that cathode rays could be deflected by an electric field in a manner consistent with negatively charged particles. This experiment also allowed the deduction that the cathode rays were not electromagnetic waves because the latter would not be deflected by an electric field.
The combined effect of changing the magnitudes of electric and magnetic fields through which the electrons passed was measured and from this the charge-to-mass ratio of the electron was calculated.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5-mark row: the answer assesses the deflection results for both the existence of electrons (charged particles, not waves) and their properties, including the charge-to-mass ratio from the combined fields. The middle answer outlines a result and links it to charge, but does not assess its strength or cover mass.

sampleAnswers.answer: Thomson's cathode-ray tube showed that cathode rays are deflected by an electric field, so they carry negative charge. This supports the view that the rays are charged particles, which are electrons.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by outlining an experiment and its result, and relating it to the existence of electrons. It does not assess how strongly the results support the claim, and it covers neither the mass of the electron nor its charge-to-mass ratio. Adding the combined-field result and the charge-to-mass ratio would lift it towards the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Electrons were found through cathode-ray experiments.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by giving some relevant information about the period and cathode rays. It describes no experiment or result, and naming the deflection experiment and its result would lift it to the 2-mark row.

prompts.question: Outline TWO ways in which Schrödinger’s model of electron behaviour is different from electron behaviour in the atomic models of Rutherford and Bohr.
markerNotes: Each difference needs a contrast: say what Rutherford or Bohr assumed, then what Schrödinger's model describes instead.
Describe the electron as a wave, with a probability of being found in a region, not as a particle in a fixed path.
Name the earlier model in each contrast, since the question asks about both Rutherford and Bohr.
commonStudentErrors: Describes Schrödinger's model without contrasting it with Rutherford or Bohr.
Says Schrödinger's electrons still move in fixed orbits, as in Bohr's model.
Gives the same difference twice in different words.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Outlines TWO ways in which Schrödinger’s model differs from those of Rutherford and Bohr
2 marks: Outlines ONE way in which Schrödinger’s model differs from those of Rutherford and Bohr; OR; Outlines TWO features of Schrödinger’s model

sampleAnswers.answer:
In contrast to Bohr’s idea of fixed orbits, Schrödinger described orbitals as probabilities of electrons as being in particular locations.
Unlike Rutherford’s model in which electrons were imagined as particles orbiting the nucleus, Schrödinger described the electrons as waves, based on the work of de Broglie.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row with two contrasts, one with Bohr's fixed orbits and one with Rutherford's particle orbits, each stated as a feature of the wave model. A middle answer lists two features without contrasting them with either earlier model.

sampleAnswers.answer: Schrödinger described electrons as waves, with positions given as probabilities. An orbital is the region where an electron is likely to be found.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by outlining two features of Schrödinger’s model: “described electrons as waves”, and orbitals as regions of probability. Neither feature is contrasted with the Rutherford or Bohr model. Contrasting them with Bohr’s fixed orbits or Rutherford’s particle orbits would lift it to the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Schrödinger developed a wave equation for electrons.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by giving relevant information about Schrödinger's work, but it gives no way in which his model differs from the others. Adding a contrast with Bohr's fixed orbits would lift it to the 2-mark row.

prompts.question: Analyse the role of experimental evidence and theoretical ideas in developing the Standard Model of matter.
markerNotes: Analysis means showing how a theory made a prediction and how an experiment tested it, not just naming particles.
Organise the examples by the Standard Model's groups: quarks, leptons and force-carrying bosons.
Show the two-way cycle: experiments refine theory, and theory guides new experiments.
commonStudentErrors: Lists particles without saying which experiment found them or what the result showed.
Describes the Standard Model as a fixed list, without the evidence that supports it.
Says the Higgs boson gives all the mass in the universe, when it gives mass to fundamental particles.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Provides a detailed analysis of how experimental evidence and theoretical ideas contributed to the development of the Standard Model of matter
5 marks: Provides an analysis of how experimental evidence and theoretical ideas contributed to the development of the Standard Model of matter
3-4 marks: Describes experiment(s) and idea(s) relating to fundamental particles and/or forces AND links these to the Standard Model of matter
2 marks: Outlines experiments and/or ideas relating to fundamental particles or forces
1 mark: Provides some relevant information

sampleAnswers.answer:
Experiments and theoretical ideas have both been critical in the development of the Standard Model of matter.
Particle accelerators have been used to verify key ideas about fundamental particles and the structure of matter. Particle accelerators allow for small wavelength ‘matter probes’ at high energies, giving high resolution for probing the structure of matter.
Examples of particle accelerator use in the development of the Standard Model include:
• Verification of the electroweak theory, which says that the electromagnetic and weak nuclear forces are a result of the same interaction.
• The discovery of a Higgs Boson, many decades after it was first proposed as necessary in explaining the mass of particles.
• Verification of the existence of quarks by showing the protons and neutrons have internal structure.
Earlier experiments used simpler equipment such as the cloud chamber which was used to discover antimatter following its earlier theoretical prediction.
Many experiments have verified earlier theoretical ideas, and these confirmations have then in turn allowed the proposal of further ideas, which have in turn later been verified by experiments.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row: the answer analyses how accelerator tests of electroweak theory, the Higgs boson and quark structure fed into the Standard Model. The middle answer describes the accelerator results and links them to the model without showing how theory and experiment shaped each other.

sampleAnswers.answer: Particle accelerators collide particles at high energies, and the collisions convert energy into mass. The results have revealed quarks, leptons and force-carrying bosons. In the late 1960s, electrons fired at protons showed that protons have internal structure. The Higgs boson, which is linked to the mass of particles, was found at CERN’s Large Hadron Collider in 2012. These discoveries fit the Standard Model, which groups all known fundamental particles into quarks, leptons and bosons.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-4 mark row by describing accelerator experiments and ideas about proton structure and the Higgs boson, and linking them to the Standard Model: “These discoveries fit the Standard Model”. It does not analyse how theory and experiment shaped each other. Adding one prediction that a collision experiment then tested would lift it to the 5-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Accelerators are used to study the smallest particles.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by giving some relevant information about particle accelerators. It names no experiment, theory or particle, and naming one particle and the experiment that found it would lift it to the 2-mark row.

prompts.question: Outline TWO methods that could be used to determine which source is the alpha emitter, and which source is the beta emitter.
markerNotes: Each method needs the observation that tells the sources apart, such as a smaller drop in count for beta than for alpha through the same material.
Two methods are required, and they must be different tests. Describing what alpha and beta particles are earns no method marks.
Deflection in a magnetic field separates the sources because alpha and beta particles carry opposite charges, so they bend in opposite directions.
commonStudentErrors: Describes what alpha and beta particles are without giving a method to tell the sources apart.
Gives two versions of the same test, such as two checks with paper, so only one method is really outlined.
States a difference, such as "the count drops", without saying which source it identifies.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Outlines TWO methods and subsequent observations that could be used to identify each source as either alpha or beta emitters
2 marks: Outlines a method that could be used to distinguish the sources; OR; Identifies TWO methods that could be used to identify each source
1 mark: Provides some relevant information

sampleAnswers.answer:
Pass the radiation through a thin material to a detector. Observe any changes in counts. The beta source count will be reduced by an amount less than the alpha source count.
Pass each type of radiation through a magnetic field and observe any differences in deflection and observe deflection in opposite directions.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row with two methods, each with the observation that tells the sources apart: penetration through a thin material and deflection in a magnetic field. A middle answer names the method but leaves out the identifying observation.

sampleAnswers.answer: Test each source in a magnetic field. Direct a narrow beam through the field and record where it strikes a detector, so the deflection of each source can be compared.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by outlining a method that could distinguish the sources: “Test each source in a magnetic field”. No observation says which source is alpha and which is beta, so neither source is identified. Stating the direction of deflection for each source would lift it to the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Alpha particles are positive helium nuclei; beta particles are electrons.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by giving relevant information about the two radiations, but it describes no method. Naming a test and the result that separates the sources would lift it to the 2-mark row.
